about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued August 28, 2008, examines the fate of used electronics exported from the United States, the effectiveness of U.S. regulatory controls over those exports, and opportunities for strengthening the federal role in regulating used electronics exports. It focuses on EPA's regulation and enforcement, particularly the 2006 cathode-ray tube (CRT) rule under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, and describes unsafe handling of exported electronics in developing countries and options such as amending RCRA regulations and ratifying the Basel Convention.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that a substantial amount of exported used electronics ends up in countries such as China and India, where they are often handled and disposed of unsafely, including by open-air burning and acid baths. Current U.S. regulatory controls do little to stem exports of potentially hazardous used electronics because most used electronics are not regulated as hazardous waste, the CRT rule is easily circumvented, and EPA has done little to enforce the rule. The report found 43 U.S. electronics recyclers willing to export broken, untested, or nonworking CRTs under conditions that would appear to violate the CRT rule, and EPA records showed none of them had filed the required notifications for recycling. EPA had not issued its first administrative penalty complaint until July 2008, had set no enforcement targets, conducted no monitoring, and had no plans or timetable for developing an enforcement strategy. The report also identifies options for strengthening the federal role, including amending RCRA regulations, ratifying the Basel Convention, improving tracking with other agencies, and updating RCRA regulations to reflect OECD obligations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: According to EPA, Americans removed more than 300 million electronic devices from their households in 2006. CRTs contain up to 4 pounds of lead. In the report's undercover exercise, GAO e-mailed 343 solicitations to electronics recyclers and trading companies, and 64 responded; 43 companies were willing to export broken, untested, or nonworking CRTs in apparent violation of the CRT rule. EPA records showed that, as of July 2008, only 1 of these 43 companies had submitted a notification for recycling. Since January 2007, Hong Kong intercepted and returned 26 shipping containers of used CRT monitors to the United States. From January to July 2008, information on six shipments, or 10 40-foot containers, of waste CRTs was provided to EPA. EPA can seek criminal penalties of up to $50,000 per day of violation and imprisonment of up to 2 years. In July 2008, EPA issued its first administrative penalty complaint seeking the maximum civil penalty of $32,500. As of August 2008, EPA reported 10 ongoing investigations, 7 of which appeared to come from GAO. On Internet e-commerce sites, GAO observed 2,234 requests to purchase LCD screens, 430 requests for central processing units, 665 requests for used computers, and 230 requests for about 7.5 million used CRTs from February 2008 to May 2008. Brokers in developing countries represented over 60 percent of the requests; over 75 percent of brokers' requests offered $10 or less per unit, and almost half offered $5 or less; about 70 percent of requests came from developing countries in Asia. As of June 2008, 25 companies had submitted 47 notices for export of CRTs for recycling. A Maryland recycler charges $10 to $30 for CRT monitors. A New York recycler purchased 221 CRT monitors from New York state surplus; a Georgia recycler purchased 100 CRT monitors for $45 and another 155 CRT monitors for $366, and offered three container-loads of untested CRT monitors, with about 850 monitors per container and up to 1,100 to 1,200 per container for an additional $400. Shipping from the United States to West Africa ranges from $4,000 to $7,000 per 20-foot container, while a 40-foot container to Hong Kong costs $750. Functional used computers in West Africa can sell for as little as $100. Scavengers in Cambodia can collect material for as little as $1 a day. More than 10,000 people work in Delhi's informal recycling industry. A United Nations University study found that the manufacturing phase takes up 80 percent of the natural resources used during the life cycle of computers. The U.S. Geological Survey reports that 1 metric ton of computer scrap contains more gold than 17 metric tons of ore. Samsung Corning's facility in Malaysia recycles CRT glass and manufactures CRT televisions containing as much as 50 percent recycled-glass content, and about 250 shipping containers totaling about 4,000 tons of CRT glass leave the United States for Malaysia each month. Umicore recycles over 95 percent of the electronic items it processes. A 2007 study found that children in Guiyu had blood lead levels more than 50 percent higher than the CDC limit for lead exposure and more than 50 percent higher than children in a neighboring village. EPA stated that consumer electronics comprise less than two percent of the municipal solid waste stream, and that between 15 and 20 percent by weight of used and end-of-life electronics are collected for reuse and recycling, with the remaining 80 to 85 percent disposed of domestically.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Administrator of EPA identify a timetable for developing and implementing a systematic plan to enforce the CRT rule, including enforcement targets, monitoring, follow-up of suspected violations, and prosecution. It also recommends that the Administrator direct the heads of appropriate offices to develop options for broadening EPA's regulations under existing RCRA authority to address exports of used electronic devices that are not classified as hazardous waste but have a high likelihood of threatening human health and the environment when unsafely disassembled, including expanding the scope of the CRT rule and revising the regulatory definition of hazardous waste. It further recommends cooperating with other federal agencies to improve tracking of exported used electronics, such as by implementing specific harmonized tariff codes. Finally, it recommends that EPA submit to Congress a legislative package for ratification of the Basel Convention.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle whether EPA will develop or implement an enforcement plan; EPA had no plans or timetable, and EPA generally disagreed with the recommendations, preferring nonregulatory, voluntary approaches. Several EPA investigations were pending at the time of the report, including the outcome of EPA's investigation of the containers returned to the Port of Los Angeles and the outcome of its investigation of a container re-exported to Hong Kong from the Port of Tacoma. The report also states that GAO does not know whether Hong Kong again intercepted that Tacoma container. The report's Internet-based findings carry stated caveats: the information presented assumes that buyers do not post fictitious country names and that there is no double counting of requests, and GAO found the data adequate only to conclude that significant demand exists for exported used electronics.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-1075R, issued September 16, 2008) on the federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards that pertain to securing privately owned information technology systems and data within the 18 critical infrastructure sectors. It identifies the applicable requirements for each sector and the enforcement mechanisms for those requirements, based on information solicited from the federal agencies responsible for overseeing each sector and GAO's review of the U.S. Code, Code of Federal Regulations, and federal mandatory standards. It also transmits the briefing slides presented to congressional staff on July 24, 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are GAO's own, based on agency-provided data and GAO's review of applicable legal sources. It found at least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards that pertain to securing privately owned IT systems and data, comprising 1 law, 25 regulations, and 8 mandatory standards, applying in 10 of the 18 critical infrastructure sectors. Eight sectors did not identify any such requirements: critical manufacturing, defense industrial base, emergency services, government facilities, information technology, national monuments and icons, postal and shipping, and telecommunications. Each of the 34 requirements has at least one enforcement mechanism, including court injunctions, civil monetary penalties, criminal penalties, and administrative actions, though these mechanisms are typically general enforcement tools rather than requirements specific to IT security. The sector-specific agencies agreed with the information and provided technical comments.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Federal policy identifies 18 critical infrastructure sectors. GAO identified at least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards: 1 law, 25 regulations, and 8 mandatory standards, applying in 10 of the 18 sectors. The count of laws excludes authorizing laws for the regulations and mandatory standards. By sector, the applicable counts are: agriculture and food, 1 regulation; banking and finance, 17 regulations; chemical, 1 regulation; commercial facilities, 1 regulation; dams, 8 mandatory standards; drinking water and water treatment systems, 1 law; energy, 1 regulation and 8 mandatory standards; nuclear reactors, materials, and waste, 1 regulation; public health and healthcare, 1 regulation; and transportation systems, 2 regulations. The dams and energy sectors share the same 8 mandatory standards, counted once. Eight sectors had no applicable requirements. Enforcement amounts and periods stated include: a civil monetary penalty of up to $1 million per day for a knowing banking and finance violation likely to cause substantial loss; a fine of up to $25,000 per violation for a community water system violation; a fine of up to $100,000 per day per violation for a nuclear reactors, materials, and waste violation; imprisonment of up to one year and a fine of up to $1,000 for the agriculture and food regulation; a fine of up to $25,000 per day for a chemical facility violation; a fine of up to $25,000 per violation for a gaming operation on Indian land; a fine of up to $50,000 and imprisonment of up to one year for knowingly disclosing individually identifiable health information; and a fine of up to $100,000 per violation for a transportation systems regulation. The briefing was presented on July 24, 2008, and the report was issued September 16, 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document states a recommendation from GAO's October 2007 report: the Secretary of Homeland Security should request that, by September 2008, the sector-specific agencies develop plans that address all of the key aspects of cyber security.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that there is a possibility that the agencies did not identify all applicable requirements and that GAO did not conduct an independent search for applicable requirements. It did not include privately owned IT systems and data operated on behalf of a federal agency, including contractor-operated systems subject to governmentwide requirements such as the Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002. The enforcement mechanisms and authorities identified are examples and do not necessarily constitute a complete list. Where GAO could not reconcile its analysis with agencies' interpretations, it reported the agencies' characterizations. It also notes that the chemical sector's risk-based performance standards have not been finalized or submitted to the Office of Management and Budget for approval and therefore are not yet enforceable.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-1123, issued September 18, 2008, to Congressional Requesters. It examines whether collaboration between the Small Business Administration (SBA) and USDA Rural Development could be improved. The report discusses the complementary nature of some SBA and Rural Development loan and business programs, past and current collaborative efforts between the two agencies and with other agencies, and opportunities to facilitate more effective collaboration in support of rural economic development.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's findings are GAO's own, based on a performance audit conducted from October 2007 to September 2008. The report finds that the complementary nature of some SBA loan programs and Rural Development business programs provides a rationale for collaboration, because both agencies serve similar rural areas and groups, offer comparable products, and have similar eligibility requirements, while also having different strengths such as faster loan processing at SBA and higher loan limits at Rural Development. It finds that collaborative efforts have been sporadic, mostly initiated at the local level, and dependent on established working relationships, with frequent formal collaboration in some locations, informal collaboration in others, and no collaboration in many states. It also finds that SBA and Rural Development lack a current cooperative agreement, did not appear to implement a December 2000 memorandum of understanding before it expired in 2003, lack formal incentives for collaboration, and do not track the results of collaborative efforts, reducing the likelihood that they will fully leverage each other's strengths.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that more than 80 federal programs target rural economic development. SBA has 68 field offices nationwide, USDA Rural Development has 47 state offices and about 500 area or local field offices, and SBA has more than 950 Small Business Development Center locations. For fiscal year 2007, SBA's 7(a) program provided more than 99,000 loans totaling nearly $14 billion; the 504 program provided about 11,000 loans totaling approximately $6 billion; the 7(m) Micro Loan Program provided about $19 million in microloans; and the Small Business Investment Company program provided over $2.5 billion in venture capital funding to more than 2,000 small businesses. For fiscal year 2007, Rural Development's Business and Industry program provided over $836 million in loan guarantees; the Intermediary Relending Program spent about $34 million; the Rural Business Enterprise Grant Program provided approximately $43 million; the Rural Business Opportunity Grant Program provided about $7 million; the Rural Economic Development Loan and Grant Program provided about $26 million in loans and about $10 million in grants; and the Renewable Energy Systems and Energy Efficiency Improvements program provided approximately $48 million in energy loans, $11 million in energy grants, and recipients received over $18 million in joint funding. The maximum 7(a) loan is $2 million, while the maximum Business and Industry loan is $25 million. The maximum guaranty for 7(a) loans is 85 percent for loans up to $150,000 and 75 percent for loans over $150,000; for Business and Industry loans the maximum guaranty is 80 percent for loans up to $5 million, 70 percent for loans between $5 million and $10 million, and 60 percent for loans over $10 million. SBA loan processing averages 5 to 7 business days, and 7(a) loans can take as little as 2 business days, while Rural Development processing takes 10 to 60 days. The Rural Lender Advantage Pilot Program offers a simplified application for loans of $350,000 or less, with SBA guaranteeing 85 percent of loan amounts up to $150,000 and 75 percent above $150,000. The 504 program's certified development company portfolio must create or retain one job for every $35,000 provided by SBA, and 7(m) microloans are up to $35,000 with an average loan size of about $13,000. Most Rural Development programs are available in areas with 50,000 or fewer people, except the Intermediary Relending Program, which is limited to areas with 25,000 or fewer. Of SBA's 68 district offices, only about half reported ongoing collaborative efforts with Rural Development, and of Rural Development's 47 state offices, only about half reported such efforts. In North Dakota, SBA and Rural Development offered at least eight joint lender trainings each year and held quarterly meetings, and officials estimated that about one of every four 504 loans in rural North Dakota communities with populations less than 25,000 had been used jointly with Intermediary Relending loans. The report also cites an example of a health care business that received a 504 loan to purchase a new $7.2 million headquarters building, employing 301 professionals, serving 760 patients daily, with annual sales over $9 million, and an Iowa Intermediary Relending award of $600,000 that assisted 7 businesses, created 200 jobs, and saved 259 jobs. Under the Rural Business Investment Program, it took about 2 years from enactment in 2002 to finalize agreements and announce funding in 2004, and only one company was able to raise the necessary capital for full approval before funding was lost in 2006.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Administrator of SBA and the Secretary of Agriculture take steps to adopt a formal approach to encourage further collaboration in support of common economic development goals in rural areas. The report says such steps could include establishing and implementing a written agreement; defining and articulating a common outcome for rural economic development; specifying roles and responsibilities to ensure proper coordination; establishing mechanisms to monitor, evaluate, and report on results; and reinforcing accountability for collaborative efforts.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that there is no commonly accepted definition of collaboration and that the report therefore defines it for its own purposes. It acknowledges that it received responses from only about half of SBA district offices and all Rural Development state offices, and that it conducted site visits at only three locations. It says SBA and Rural Development headquarters officials were not able to provide examples of collaborative efforts when first asked, and that the agencies did not appear to agree for a period of months about whether the December 2000 memorandum of understanding was active. The report does not settle whether the 2000 memorandum would have been effective if implemented, stating only that the agencies do not appear to have implemented it and giving two possible reasons: a change in USDA administration and a lack of active monitoring. It also notes that the success of the Rural Business Investment Program was limited due to a lack of funding.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued September 17, 2008, is a follow-up audit of the Department of Health and Human Services' (HHS) efforts to define and implement an overall approach for protecting the privacy of electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network. It updates progress since a January 2007 GAO report, assesses HHS actions against GAO's recommendations, and concludes that although HHS has taken important steps, it has not fully implemented an overall privacy approach because it has not defined a process for ensuring all key privacy principles and challenges are fully and adequately addressed.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are GAO's own. Since January 2007, HHS has undertaken various initiatives contributing to an overall privacy approach, including standards, certification criteria, and state-level collaborations. HHS fulfilled the first part of GAO's recommendation by identifying milestones and assigning responsibility for integrating privacy-related outcomes and developing a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework. However, HHS has not fulfilled the rest in full: it has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. Without such a process, HHS faces the risk that privacy protection measures may not be consistently and effectively built into health IT programs, jeopardizing patient privacy and public trust. HHS generally agreed with the report but neither agreed nor disagreed with the recommendation, and stated it is actively pursuing a two-phased process for assessing and prioritizing privacy-related initiatives.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report cites a September 2007 Institute of Medicine survey in which nearly 60 percent of respondents did not believe that the privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected. President Bush issued an executive order in April 2004 calling for widespread adoption of interoperable electronic health records within 10 years. HHS awarded four health IT contracts in 2005. In January 2007, four test network implementations, or prototypes, demonstrated potential nationwide health information exchange. A state-level consortium issued reports in February 2007 and March 2008. The Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup submitted recommendations in February and April 2008. The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics submitted five recommendations in February 2008. The State Alliance for e-Health's information protection task force proposed five recommendations in August 2007. The Secretary released the federal health IT strategic plan in June 2008, with strategies to complete a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by the end of 2008 and to address inconsistent statutes or regulations by the end of 2011; the framework is expected to be published by December 2008. HHS's comments state the President's goal that most Americans have secure electronic health records by 2014. The audit was conducted from April 2008 through September 2008. The strategic plan covers 2008-2012. HHS awarded contracts to nine health information exchange organizations and cooperative agreements to six additional organizations. The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics was established in 1949, and the Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup was formed in 2006.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders, to ensure that key privacy principles and challenges are fully and adequately addressed. No other recommendations are made.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether HHS's privacy approach will fully address all key privacy principles and challenges; it states that HHS has not defined a process for ensuring this. It notes that recommendations from the Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup and the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics are still under consideration by the Secretary. It also reports that HHS neither agreed nor disagreed with the recommendation and that more work remains.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-180, issued June 27, 2008, titled 'Homeland Security: First Responders' Ability to Detect and Model Hazardous Releases in Urban Areas Is Significantly Limited.' It examines the limitations of the tools local first responders have for responding to airborne chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) releases in urban areas, specifically detection equipment and plume models, and the information available on how such releases affect urban populations. It addresses four questions: the limitations of detection equipment; what DHS has done to develop and adopt performance standards and test equipment; the limitations of plume models in urban environments; and what information is available on the effects of exposure to CBRN materials. The report makes recommendations to the Secretary of Homeland Security.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that, more than six years after September 11, 2001, local first responders still lack tools that can accurately and quickly identify CBRN releases in urban environments. Radiological and nuclear detection equipment can detect the presence of significant amounts of material but cannot predict atmospheric dispersion, and no federal agency has the mission to develop, test, and certify radiological atmospheric detection equipment for first responders. Chemical detectors are generally inadequate for detecting chemical warfare agents at less-than-lethal but still harmful concentrations, and handheld biological detectors are not reliable; BioWatch does not provide real-time detection, with confirmation taking several hours to more than a day and no determination of quantity. DHS had adopted only 4 performance standards for CBRN detection equipment out of 39 total standards as of October 30, 2007, none for chemical or biological detection, and does not independently test manufacturers' claims. Nonurban and urban plume models have significant limitations in complex urban environments, have not been adequately validated, can produce contradictory results, and cannot provide ground truth or certain source-term estimates. Significant data gaps exist on low-level exposure effects, especially for vulnerable urban populations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports the following figures: in the 2001 anthrax attack, 22 persons contracted anthrax disease and 5 died in four states and Washington, D.C. In a sarin-release planning scenario, an estimated 6,000 people are killed and economic damages are $300 million. The 1984 Bhopal release killed approximately 3,800 people. In the January 6, 2005 Graniteville, South Carolina chlorine release, 11,500 gallons of chlorine gas were released, 9 people died (8 from inhaling chlorine gas), at least 529 people sought medical care, and 5,453 residents were evacuated. Approximately 800,000 shipments of hazardous materials travel daily in the United States. As of October 30, 2007, DHS had adopted 39 total standards, including 4 for radiation detection equipment and none for chemical or biological detection equipment. DHS assessed ion mobility spectrometer and surface acoustic wave sensitivities for V and G nerve agents at approximately 2 ppb to 20 ppb, with limits of detection of 200 ppb to 300 ppb for blister agents; electrochemical cell sensitivities range from ppb to low ppm. DHS BioWatch spending for fiscal years 2005 through 2007 was about $236 million, with more than 30 jurisdictions participating; real-time detection has been defined as 30 seconds or less. In the states visited, Washington state agencies, hazmat teams, and local fire departments in 11 counties acquired CBRN detection equipment with about $3.2 million of SHSP and UASI grant funds in 2004-2005; Seattle alone spent about $500,000; Connecticut spent about $1.8 million in DHS grants for CBRN detection equipment in 2003-2005. Standards generally take 3 to 5 years to achieve consensus, though DHS noted radiation detection and powder sampling standards were developed in 12 to 18 months. As of October 2007, the Responder Knowledge Base included 1,127 certifications for equipment on DHS's authorized equipment list and 268 reports of operational suitability testing. In one Washington State test, a new brand of digital dosimeters read consistently only 40 percent of what current dosimeters read. CAMEO/ALOHA includes a database for over 6,000 chemicals and does not make predictions for distances greater than 6.2 miles (10 kilometers) or for more than one hour after a release begins. NARAC and IMAAC can provide an automated prediction for CBRN events within 5 to 15 minutes. An interagency study evaluated 29 modeling systems, and OFCM reported that most of the more than 140 documented modeling systems are limited in their ability to accurately predict plume path and contamination in urban environments.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security take four actions: reach agreement with DOD, DOE, EPA, and other agencies on which agency should have the mission and responsibility to develop, independently test, and certify detection equipment first responders can use to detect hazardous material releases in the atmosphere; ensure that manufacturers' claims are independently tested and validated regarding whether commercial off-the-shelf CBRN detection equipment can detect given hazardous material at specific sensitivities; refine IMAAC's procedures by working with other federal, state, and local agencies to develop common/joint IMAAC emergency response practices including procedures for dealing with contradictory plume modeling information, refine the concept of operations for chemical, biological, and radiological releases, and delineate the type and scale of major CBRN incidents that would qualify for IMAAC assistance; and, in conjunction with IMAAC, work with the federal plume modeling community to accelerate research and development to address plume model deficiencies in urban areas and improve federal modeling and assessment capabilities, including improvements to meteorological information, plume models, and data sets to evaluate plume models. DHS concurred with the recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that interagency studies concluded that plume models have not been adequately validated for homeland security applications and are not designed for complex built-up urban environments; an NRC study found no one model had all features deemed critical. Urban plume models show an unpredictable range of uncertainty and cannot give first responders ground truth or determine source term with certainty, particularly for toxic industrial chemicals. It identifies significant data gaps on how CBRN releases affect urban populations, including a severe lack of scientific research on low-level exposure effects for vulnerable populations such as elderly people, children, and individuals with compromised immune systems, and the absence of dose-response parameters for the general population for most chemical warfare agents. The document notes that DHS's testing mission is limited to equipment DHS is developing and does not extend to commercial equipment; that DHS relies on manufacturers' claims and anecdotal information; that SAVER assessments do not include independent scientific testing; and that reference guides do not contain testing data validating manufacturers' claims. It reports that BioWatch is qualitative, not quantitative, and cannot determine how much material was released. The document also notes caveats raised by commenters: DHS said GAO should consider alternative scenarios in which first responders are assisted by state and federal agencies, while GAO's report considered first responders on the scene before federal assets arrive; and DOC said that even with implementation of the recommendations, plume models would still have limitations as a primary tool. It also notes that handheld immunoassay manufacturers expressed concern about the methods, objectivity, and overall quality of the CDC/FBI evaluation study on which OSTP's recommendation against their use was based.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: U.S. congressional requesters — the Senate and House committee leaders listed in the report — to support congressional oversight of and decisions about DHS programs for first responders' CBRN detection and modeling capabilities.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: GAO-08-432 is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to the Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, Federal Services, and International Security of the U.S. Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. It examines undisbursed grant balances remaining in expired grant accounts in the largest federal civilian grant payment system, HHS's Payment Management System (PMS), from 2003 through 2006, identifies common program characteristics of those accounts, assesses grants management challenges affecting grant closeout, and recommends executive branch actions.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that about $1 billion in undisbursed funding remained in expired grant accounts in PMS during calendar year 2006, representing about 1 percent of total funds made available for all expired grant accounts in PMS; when accounts with no funds remaining were excluded, undisbursed funding averaged about 26 percent of original funding. Expired grant accounts with undisbursed funds were associated with thousands of grantees and over 325 federal grant programs. The largest undisbursed balances were consistently in mid-range awards, project-based grants, and grants to state organizations, although these results could not be compared with all closed federal grants. Dozens of past audit reports and agency performance reports showed that undisbursed balances in expired grant accounts were a long-standing challenge caused by low closeout priority, inconsistent procedures, poorly timed communications with grantees, and insufficient compliance or enforcement. When agencies such as DOJ's OJP, HHS's NIH, and EPA made concerted efforts, auditors reported improved timeliness of closeouts and reduced undisbursed balances. GAO also found that OMB circulars did not instruct agencies to track and report on expired grants and undisbursed grant funding.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that during calendar year 2006 about $1 billion in undisbursed funding remained in expired grant accounts in PMS, which handled about 70 percent of all federal grant disbursements in 2006. This was about 1 percent of total funds made available for all expired grant accounts in PMS during 2006, and about 26 percent of original funding on average when expired accounts with no funds remaining were excluded. Quarterly undisbursed funding in expired grant accounts increased from about $600 million in 2003 to about $1 billion during 2006; from March 2003 through March 2005 the average ranged between 14 and 16 percent of funds made available, and from June 2005 through December 2006 it ranged between 24 and 26 percent. In 15 of 16 quarters, at least four federal departments using PMS had over 100 expired grant accounts with undisbursed funding, and over 325 programs and thousands of grantees were associated with these accounts. The largest quarterly balances were in accounts with funding awards from over $100,000 to $100 million. Federal grant awards to nonfederal entities increased from $300 billion to over $450 billion from 2000 through 2006, and grants represented about one-sixth of the federal budget. The report also states that EPA closed out only 37 percent of grants in fiscal year 2005 within 180 days; DOJ OIG reported $172 million in undisbursed funding could have been deobligated; Operation Closeout closed 4,136 grants and deobligated over $30 million; OJP reduced its backlog of expired grants from 11,356 to 6,237 from 2001 to 2005; HHS reported more than 64,000 grants with a remaining balance of $1.6 billion eligible for closeout, with 75 percent expired for more than 2 years; and EPA reported a 95 percent grant closure rate against a 90 percent goal. In 2006 PMS processed over $320 billion in payments, contained over 200,000 open grants as of June 2007, and open grants represented over $1.3 trillion as of May 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of OMB instruct all executive departments and independent agencies to annually track the amount of undisbursed grant funding remaining in expired grant accounts and report on the status and resolution of that funding in their annual performance plan and annual Performance and Accountability Report, including the amount of undisbursed grant funding, why the funds were undisbursed, actions taken to resolve the undisbursed funding and close the expired grants and related accounts, and outcomes associated with those actions. The report also presents OMB's response: OMB supported the intent but did not commit to implementing the recommendations and did not favor requiring agencies to report these balances in their PARs.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that its results on program characteristics could not be compared with all closed federal grants or all closed grants in PMS because of the burden of collecting comparable data from the eight other federal civilian payment systems, so GAO could not know whether the characteristics represented a disproportionate share. It notes that each program-characteristic analysis was independent and the results cannot be combined into a general statement; that GAO did not interview policy experts or agency grant managers to explore why different characteristics had larger undisbursed balances; and that the report did not evaluate implementation of closeout procedures for any specific grant program or awarding agency. The report also says data analysis of grant accounts in other federal payment systems may reveal additional expired grants with undisbursed balances. OMB did not commit to implementing the recommendations and said it would consider revising its grants management guidance during its regular review.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, Federal Services, and International Security of the U.S. Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and copies were sent to congressional committees with jurisdiction over HHS, the Secretary of HHS, and the Director of OMB; it supports oversight and decisions on increasing accountability and transparency for unspent federal grant funds.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-525, issued June 27, 2008, titled 'Information Security: Federal Agency Efforts to Encrypt Sensitive Information Are Under Way, but Work Remains.' It examines how commercially available encryption technologies can help federal agencies protect sensitive information and reduce risks, the federal laws, policies, and guidance governing encryption use, and the extent to which 24 major federal agencies had implemented or planned to implement encryption to protect sensitive information. The scope includes a survey of 24 major federal agencies and tests of encryption practices at 6 selected agencies, conducted from February 2007 through June 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that many types of commercially available encryption technologies can help agencies protect stored and transmitted sensitive information, but incorrect implementation can create a false sense of security or make data permanently inaccessible. Federal laws do not specifically require encryption, but FISMA, the Privacy Act, the E-Government Act, HIPAA, and the Veterans Benefits, Health Care, and Information Technology Act frame information protection responsibilities. OMB recommended in M-06-16 that agencies encrypt all data on mobile computers and devices and, in M-07-16, restated that recommendation as a requirement and required the use of NIST-certified cryptographic modules. All 24 surveyed agencies had initiated encryption efforts, but none had completed them or documented comprehensive implementation plans, and 18 had not completed inventories of sensitive information. Encryption of stored data on mobile devices lagged behind encryption of transmitted data: agencies reported that about 70 percent of laptop computers and handheld devices had not been encrypted. Most agencies reported encrypting nearly all or all transmitted sensitive information over wired Internet and wireless networks. Tests at 6 agencies found weaknesses in installing and configuring FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, monitoring effectiveness, developing policies and procedures, and training personnel. As a result, GAO concluded sensitive federal information remains at increased risk of unauthorized disclosure, modification, or loss.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports that in 2006 the Department of Veterans Affairs reported a stolen unencrypted laptop and external hard drive containing the personal information of approximately 26.5 million veterans and U.S. military personnel. It cites a February 2008 theft of a laptop containing personally identifiable information for as many as 4,000 participants in the Marine Corps' New Parent Support Program, a December 2007 Energy Department intrusion via an e-mail-embedded program, and a May 2007 missing external hard drive containing personal data for 100,000 archived employment records at the Transportation Security Administration. Incidents reported to US-CERT increased from 3,634 in fiscal year 2005 to 5,503 in fiscal year 2006 and 13,029 in fiscal year 2007, about a 259 percent increase. The survey covered 24 major federal agencies, and testing covered 6 agencies. Among the 24 agencies reporting from July through September 2007, 8 reported encrypting information on less than 20 percent of laptop and handheld devices, 5 on 20 to 39 percent, 2 on 40 to 59 percent, 3 on 60 to 79 percent, and 6 on 80 to 100 percent; overall, about 70 percent of laptop computers and handheld devices had not been encrypted. Of 22 agencies, 10 reported encrypting less than 20 percent of portable storage media taken offsite and 3 reported 20 to 39 percent; of 17 agencies, 9 reported encrypting less than 20 percent of offsite backup storage media. Six agencies reported other storage devices that could contain sensitive data, 4 had not encrypted these devices, and officials at 1 agency had no plans to encrypt sensitive data on portable media. Of 23 agencies reporting on wired Internet transmissions, 18 reported encrypting 80 to 100 percent; of 21 agencies reporting on wireless transmissions, 12 reported 80 to 100 percent. At the 6 tested agencies, 2 had not installed FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, 4 had not configured installed encryption technologies according to FIPS 140-2, all 6 had not developed or documented encryption management policies and procedures, and 3 had not adequately trained personnel. Education had not installed a FIPS-validated product on any of the 15 laptop computers tested; USDA, State, and GSA had installed FIPS-compliant technologies on all 58 laptop computers tested; NASA's software was installed on 27 of 29 tested laptops; and a USDA component had not effectively monitored encryption on 5 of 52 tested laptops. One of three virtual private networks installed by Education was not FIPS-compliant, and two agencies had not configured their virtual private networks to use only strong, FIPS-validated encryption algorithms. Four of the 6 agencies lacked a policy for encryption key establishment and management, and none of the 6 had detailed procedures for that control. The report makes 20 recommendations: 2 to OMB, 3 to USDA, 5 to Education, 3 to HUD, 2 to State, 2 to GSA, and 3 to NASA.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes 20 recommendations for executive action. It recommends that the Director of OMB take two actions: clarify governmentwide policy requiring agencies to encrypt sensitive agency data through additional guidance and/or educational activities, and monitor the effectiveness of agencies' encryption implementation plans and efforts to inventory sensitive information they hold. It recommends that the Secretary of Agriculture direct the chief information officer to establish and implement a mechanism to monitor the successful installation and effective functioning of encryption products; develop and implement departmentwide procedures for encryption key establishment and management; and develop and implement a training program for technical support and end-user personnel. It recommends that the Secretary of Education direct the chief information officer to evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products for all encryption needs and document an implementation plan; configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated cryptographic module security settings; develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography; and develop and implement a training program. It recommends that the Secretary of HUD direct the chief information officer to evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products and document an implementation plan; configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated security settings; and develop and implement departmentwide procedures for FIPS-compliant cryptography and encryption key establishment and management. It recommends that the Secretary of State direct the chief information officer to develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management and departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography. It makes the same two recommendations to the Administrator of GSA. It recommends that the NASA Administrator direct the chief information officer to establish and implement a mechanism to monitor the successful installation and effective functioning of encryption products; develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; and develop and implement a training program.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that agencies reported uncertainty regarding the applicability of OMB's encryption requirements, and OMB's later clarification that 'mobile computers and devices' includes laptops, handheld devices, and portable storage devices was not clear in its memorandums. It also states OMB did not provide evidence that it monitored agencies' efforts to inventory the sensitive information they hold or to develop implementation plans. It reports that none of the 24 agencies had documented comprehensive encryption implementation plans, and 18 had not completed inventories of sensitive information. It notes that at USDA, a system administrator attributed unencrypted drives to a failed activation step and the agency had no mechanism to monitor whether the product was functioning; NASA had no mechanism to detect whether encryption was successfully installed and functioning; three agencies had not enabled BlackBerry content protection because of operational issues and were awaiting a vendor solution; some NASA users refused installation or were unfamiliar with the product; some Education users were unaware encryption software was installed; and NASA had no mechanism to track whether users completed required training. The report does not settle whether these weaknesses will be resolved; it states that until they are addressed, sensitive federal information will remain at increased risk.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to Congressional Requesters: the Honorable Bennie G. Thompson, Chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security; the Honorable Jane Harman, Chairwoman of the Subcommittee on Intelligence, Information Sharing and Terrorism Risk Assessment; and the Honorable Zoe Lofgren. It supports congressional oversight of federal agency information security and encryption efforts.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-538, issued August 15, 2008) assesses U.S. Customs and Border Protection's (CBP) efforts to promote international supply chain security standards through the World Customs Organization (WCO). It addresses three questions: what actions CBP has taken to develop and implement international supply chain security standards; what actions CBP has taken with international partners to achieve mutual recognition of customs security practices; and what issues CBP and foreign customs administrations anticipate in implementing 100 percent scanning of U.S.-bound container cargo. The report covers the SAFE Framework, CSI, C-TPAT, the Secure Freight Initiative, and mutual recognition arrangements.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that CBP took a lead role, with 11 other WCO members, in developing the WCO SAFE Framework, which was adopted in June 2005 by the WCO's 173 member customs administrations and is based on CBP's CSI and C-TPAT programs. CBP assisted in implementing the SAFE Framework through capacity-building technical assistance and training, and its CSI and C-TPAT programs served as models for similar programs in other countries. CBP worked toward mutual recognition of customs-to-business partnership programs, signing arrangements with New Zealand in June 2007 and with Jordan and Canada in June 2008, and agreed with the European Commission to establish mutual recognition by early 2009. The report also finds that the statutory requirement to scan 100 percent of U.S.-bound container cargo by 2012 may affect worldwide adoption of international standards: international partners told DHS and Congress it runs counter to the SAFE Framework, it is unclear who will pay for additional resources, and officials from CBP and European customs administrations said it could provide a lower level of security by diluting the focus on high-risk containers.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: GAO-08-538 is a 58-page report issued August 15, 2008. In fiscal year 2007, 11 million oceangoing cargo containers arrived at U.S. seaports—roughly 30,000 per day—from more than 700 foreign seaports. The WCO represents the customs administrations of 173 countries; its SAFE Framework was adopted in June 2005 by the 173 member customs administrations. As of June 2008, 154 WCO member countries had signed letters of intent to implement the SAFE Framework. There were 58 CSI seaports in 33 countries; as of July 2008, 2 of the 33 participating countries (Canada and Japan) had decided to station their customs officers in U.S. seaports. As of May 2008, C-TPAT had over 8,400 members. As of April 2008, 111 countries were participating in the WCO capacity-building program; as of July 2008, 104 had completed the first phase, 65 had moved into the second phase, and 1 was in the third phase. CBP had provided training and assistance to 10 countries in the capacity-building program. According to WCO data, about 70 countries had begun developing their own national AEO programs. In a 2002 simulated scenario, detonation of weapons smuggled in cargo containers shut down all U.S. seaports for 12 days and could result in a loss of $58 billion to the U.S. economy. The 9/11 Act requires 100 percent scanning of all U.S.-bound container cargo by 2012. The SAFE Framework includes 11 customs-to-customs standards and 6 customs-to-business standards. The Revised Kyoto Convention is an international customs agreement signed by 55 countries, including the United States; the report later states the European Commission, the United States, and 52 other nations have acceded to it. The Secure Freight Initiative pilot program was conducted at six selected CSI seaports. Under the U.S.-EU action plan, a transshipment pilot was completed in 2006; a feeder port pilot ran at the Port of Szczecin, Poland, from March 2007 to September 2007; a 6-month pilot began in Aarhus, Denmark, in April 2008; and a 6-month pilot in Salerno, Italy, was to begin in July 2008. Two EU liaison officers were stationed at the National Targeting Center-Cargo on April 14, 2008, and the next two were to deploy on July 14, 2008, out of a total of six.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that the SFI pilot program was still under way and its full impacts were still unknown. It says the results from visits to the six CSI seaports cannot be generalized beyond the seaports visited because statistical sampling was not used, and the perspectives of foreign officials cannot be generalized across the wider population of countries. It also states it is unclear who will pay for the additional resources—staff, equipment, and infrastructure—needed for 100 percent scanning, and that officials from CBP, the WCO, and the European Commission said 100 percent scanning may provide a lower level of security than risk-based targeting. The report notes that specific details of how mutual recognition arrangements will be implemented, such as which benefits would be allotted to members of other countries' AEO programs, were being worked out, and that hurdles such as verification of inspection and targeting programs existed before CBP personnel could be removed from European seaports. An official from the WCO Private Sector Consultative Group stated that more clarity is needed between the two types of mutual recognition and the benefits associated with each.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a June 2008 U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-598) on nuclear security. It assesses the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's progress in implementing recommendations from GAO's August 2003 report on radioactive sealed sources, other steps NRC has taken to monitor and track radioactive materials, Customs and Border Protection's ability to detect radioactive materials at ports of entry on the northern and southern borders, and CBP's ability to verify that such materials are appropriately licensed before entering the United States. The context is preventing terrorists from obtaining radioactive materials to build a radiological dispersal device, or dirty bomb.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings include the following. NRC has implemented three of the six recommendations from GAO's 2003 report: identifying the highest-risk radionuclides of concern, establishing increased controls for category 2 or greater quantities of those radionuclides, and adding performance criteria for evaluating implementation. NRC has made limited progress on the other three recommendations: licensing-process weaknesses remain, because GAO investigators posing as a fictitious business obtained an NRC license and commitments from companies to sell devices that together contained a potentially dangerous quantity of a radionuclide of concern; NRC has not determined how to mitigate the potential psychological effects of an RDD; and NRC has not decided whether certain radioactive sources should be regulated through specific licenses rather than general licenses. NRC created an interim database for category 1 and 2 sources, but the National Source Tracking System has been delayed by 18 months and is not currently expected to launch until January 2009, with expansion to category 3 and larger category 4 sources slipping from July 31, 2009 to at least March 2010. The Web-based licensing system is more than 3 years behind schedule and may initially omit agreement state data, and the license verification system is in early development. CBP has a comprehensive radiation detection system at land ports, but personal radiation detectors are in short supply. CBP's May 2006 guidance requiring officers to contact the National Targeting Center whenever more than incidental, trace amounts of radiation are detected was not communicated to the field; almost all officers cited the 2003 directive as current, and at one port large neutron-emitting shipments entered the country without license verification.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report gives these figures, with units and periods as in the source: GAO-08-598, issued June 19, 2008, 53 pages; about 2 million sealed sources licensed for use in the United States; 35 agreement states; approximately 22,000 specific materials licenses, of which NRC administers about 3,750 and agreement states administer the rest; 16 radionuclides of concern; IAEA category 2 thresholds in curies for the 16 radionuclides: americium-241, 16; americium-241/beryllium, 16; californium-252, 5.4; cesium-137, 27; cobalt-60, 8.1; curium-244, 14; gadolinium-153, 270; iridium-192, 22; plutonium-238, 16; plutonium-239/beryllium, 16; promethium-147, 11,000; radium-226, 11; selenium-75, 54; strontium-90 (yttrium-90), 270; thulium-170, 5,400; ytterbium-169, 81. Also: about 1,100 of 1,700 licensees had preliminary increased-controls inspections; 22 of 35 agreement states and one of three NRC regional offices had aspects of implementation assessed; a 12-item prelicensing checklist; supplemental interim prelicensing guidance issued 12 days after NRC stopped issuing specific licenses; approximately 2 years for the general-license rulemaking, with agreement states possibly having up to an additional 3 years to implement changes, meaning full implementation could be as late as the fall of 2012; interim database established October 2003, initially a one-time snapshot for fiscal year 2004, with data 0 to 12 months old; 99 percent of licensees included in the interim database; 20 radionuclides to be tracked by the National Source Tracking System, including the 16 radionuclides of concern plus actinium-227, polonium-210, and thorium-228 and -229; NSTS originally to be operational in mid-2007, delayed by 18 months, current launch estimate January 31, 2009; expansion proposed April 2008, planned for July 31, 2009, then at least March 2010; transactions due by the close of the next business day; Web-based licensing system originally to be deployed in 2005, now no earlier than late summer 2010; agreement states represent over 80 percent of all U.S. licenses for these materials; over 90 percent of personally owned vehicles entering at land ports pass through radiation portal monitors; approximately 1,500 personal radiation detectors needed now, approximately 2,000 additional for planned new officers, leaving a shortfall of about 3,500; December 2003 radiation detection program directive, with review scheduled for December 2006 but delayed; May 2006 supplemental memorandum; CBP comment due date March 31, 2009.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Chairman of the NRC take steps, consistent with sound systems development practices, to (1) ensure priority attention is given to meeting the current January 2009 and summer 2010 target dates for launching the National Source Tracking System, Web-based licensing system, and the new license verification system, respectively; and (2) complete the steps needed to include all potentially dangerous radioactive sources, meaning category 3 and the larger category 4 sources as well as categories 1 and 2, in the National Source Tracking System as quickly as is reasonably possible. GAO also recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Commissioner of CBP to (1) effectively communicate current CBP guidance to officers at ports of entry regarding when they are required to contact the National Targeting Center to verify that radioactive materials are legitimately licensed, and (2) take measures to ensure that this guidance is being followed. The report also states that NRC should implement the remaining recommendations from GAO's 2003 report: correct the vulnerabilities in its materials licensing process, determine whether certain radioactive sources should be regulated through specific licenses rather than general licenses, and work with DHS, other federal agencies, and agreement states to determine how to effectively mitigate the potential psychological effects of an RDD event.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that NRC has not yet decided whether certain radioactive sources need stronger licensing requirements and that it is too early to evaluate whether NRC's post-2007 licensing-security steps will be successful. It says NRC has not yet determined how to effectively mitigate the potential psychological effects of an RDD and has not established firm completion dates for the license verification system. The report says it is impossible to predict what form a revised rule on general licenses would take, and that any rule change may not be fully implemented until the fall of 2012. CBP could not give a firm date for when an updated directive incorporating the May 2006 memorandum would be issued. The report also notes that its port-of-entry visits were a nonprobability sample and that the review of the 2003 directive was delayed pending resolution of unrelated matters regarding CBP's right to search property for radioactive materials between ports of entry. It questions whether NRC's target dates will again be extended and whether NRC is firmly committed to delivering the systems.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a May 30, 2008, U.S. Government Accountability Office report to the Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight, Committee on Science and Technology, House of Representatives. It examines the Department of Energy's Office of Science, specifically the extent to which Science managed its projects within cost and schedule commitments from fiscal year 2003 through fiscal year 2007, the key factors affecting that performance, and the main challenges that could affect future performance. The review covered 42 projects at 10 national laboratories, including a more detailed nongeneralizable sample of 12 projects at four laboratories.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that more than two-thirds of the 42 reviewed projects adhered to their original cost and schedule targets. Of the 27 completed projects, 24 (89 percent) were completed within their original committed cost and 21 (78 percent) were completed on or ahead of schedule; 2 (7 percent) were both over budget and late. Of the 15 projects still under way as of the end of February 2008, 9 (60 percent) were on track to meet both their cost and schedule commitments, 4 were expected to finish late, and 2 were expected to miss both. GAO attributes Science's performance to leadership commitment to meeting cost and schedule targets, appropriate management and technical expertise, and disciplined and rigorous project oversight, with occasional trimming of project scope also helping but raising concerns. GAO identifies two main future challenges: heightened funding and market uncertainties, and a shrinking pool of experienced staff due to expected retirements.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Numbers in the document include: the Office of Science had a $4 billion annual budget. GAO reviewed 42 projects at 10 national laboratories from fiscal year 2003 through fiscal year 2007; 27 projects were completed and 15 were still under way as of the end of February 2008. Of the 27 completed projects, 24 (89 percent) met their original cost targets and 21 (78 percent) were completed on or ahead of schedule; 2 (7 percent) were both over budget and late. Of the 15 ongoing projects, 9 (60 percent) were on track to meet both cost and schedule commitments, 4 (27 percent) were expected to meet cost but not schedule, and 2 (13 percent) were expected to miss both. The 12 projects reviewed in depth represented about $2.9 billion, or 75 percent, of the total value of the 42 projects. Example project figures include a Run IIb CDF Detector completed for around $10.9 million, 64 percent less than the $30.4 million cost target, and 4 months ahead of schedule; a $72 million Center for Nanoscale Materials at Argonne completed on schedule in 47 months; a $7.2 million HVAC upgrade at Oak Ridge finished 4 months early for about $150,000 less than target; a $168 million Neutrinos at the Main Injector project completed 17 months late at more than 23 percent over committed cost; and a $58 million SPEAR 3 Upgrade completed 14 months late and nearly 18 percent over its original $49 million target. The U.S. contribution to the Large Hadron Collider totaled $531 million; Science conducted 17 reviews of each of the three components, and each project was or will be completed within 2 percent of committed cost. The National Compact Stellarator Experiment was facing a likely cost increase of 91 percent and a delay of 4.5 years. Science's workforce retirement eligibility was estimated at 21 percent in 2005, increasing to 43 percent by 2011, and staffing levels at Science declined by almost 15 percent since 1999. For fiscal year 2008, $10.7 million was provided for the U.S. contribution to the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor, rather than the $160 million requested.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretary of Energy direct the Director of the Office of Engineering and Construction Management to consider whether other DOE program offices would benefit from adopting selected practices from Science's independent project reviews, such as the frequency and focus of reviews for technically complex projects. GAO also recommends that the Secretary direct that office to review DOE's project management guidance and consider whether it could be strengthened to help ensure that each project's technical goals, including expected scientific performance and corresponding facility requirements, are clearly and sufficiently defined. DOE generally agreed with the findings and said it would consider incorporating the recommendations into its Root Cause Analysis: Corrective Action Plan.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that its in-depth review of 12 projects was a nongeneralizable sample and cannot be used to make inferences about Science's overall project performance. GAO did not consider DOE's Project Assessment Reporting System fully reliable and therefore obtained project cost and schedule data directly from the laboratories. The document does not settle the effect of scope reductions on technical goals: the DOE Inspector General and the Office of Science disagreed over whether trimming the Spallation Neutron Source's planned scientific instruments compromised the project's technical goals, in part because the goals were so broadly defined that it was unclear how acquiring 5 instruments rather than the original 10 affected performance. It also notes that no contractor laboratory had yet estimated the shortfall in project management and scientific expertise from future retirements, because comprehensive workforce analyses had not been completed. DOE's Office of Engineering and Construction Management was considering issuing additional guidance on defining projects' technical goals, perhaps by 2009.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report provides the congressional appropriations subcommittees with information on the Department of Energy's management of costs and liabilities for its contractors' pension and postretirement benefit plans. It covers DOE's analysis supporting its approval of the April 2006 policy changes in Notice 351.1, the distribution of DOE's liabilities between defined benefit pension and postretirement plan components and among its management and operating and other site contracts, and DOE's recent actions to manage its future costs and liabilities. It also describes the background of DOE's reimbursement of contractor benefit costs, including DOE Order 350.1 and the suspension of Notice 351.1.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The documentation DOE provided demonstrates that DOE recognized the historical and possible future trend of its liabilities and costs related to contractor benefit plans, but DOE officials acknowledged that there was no formal compiled record or summary analysis of the documentation and factors considered before Notice 351.1 was issued. GAO found only limited evidence that DOE had considered policy alternatives, stakeholder sensitivities, or the near- and long-term financial and mission impacts of the changes, and the decision document reflecting the Deputy Secretary's approval did not include the basis on which approval was recommended. DOE suspended Notice 351.1 in June 2006 and decided not to reissue it, so Order 350.1 remains DOE's controlling policy. Since 2005, DOE has awarded 14 contracts containing provisions that limit pension and postretirement benefits for new employees to no more than 105 percent of comparable organizations, applying this provision primarily to new employees. Contractors at NNSA and Environmental Management facilities have generally established separate benefit plans for new employees that usually do not include a defined benefit pension plan, while Office of Science contractors have generally retained a single set of benefit plans. DOE expects these provisions will not substantially affect pension and postretirement benefits costs and liabilities for the next 20 to 30 years. DOE disagreed with GAO's finding that Notice 351.1 was not based on considered analysis, and GAO maintained its position.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: DOE currently has 43 contracts for facilities that cost over $16 billion annually. In 2007, DOE's financial statements reported that contractors contributed $387 million and $334 million to defined benefit pension and postretirement plans, respectively, and reported a net liability of $69.5 million for defined benefit pensions and $10.3 billion for postretirement benefits. As of September 30, 2007, benefit obligations for DOE contractors' defined benefit pension and postretirement plans were approximately $27.5 billion and $10.5 billion, respectively, with assets of $27.4 billion and $161.6 million, resulting in a net funded status of $69.5 million and $10.3 billion for the pension and postretirement plans. The net funded status of contractor pension plans changed from an underfunding of $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2006 to an underfunding of $69.5 million in fiscal year 2007, and from fiscal years 1997 to 2007 the net funded status of contractor postretirement benefits generally declined from an underfunding of $5.0 billion to $10.3 billion. At the end of fiscal year 2007, 12 defined benefit pension plans were overfunded and 34 were underfunded; the overfunded plans represented $1.9 billion in pension overfunding, with 11 overfunded plans sponsored by NNSA and Office of Science contractors representing 98 percent of that amount, and the underfunded plans represented $2.0 billion in underfunding, with 9 plans sponsored by Office of Environmental Management contractors representing 61 percent of that amount. Since 2005, DOE awarded 14 contracts with the new benefit provisions: 2 by NNSA, 6 by Environmental Management, and 6 by the Office of Science. The report also notes that four reviewed plan changes included one that increased pension obligations by almost $4 million, one that reduced retiree health obligations by $105.8 million, and two that reduced retiree life insurance obligations by a total of $112.3 million.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether DOE's issuance of Notice 351.1 was based on adequate considered analysis; DOE disagreed with GAO's finding and GAO disagreed with DOE's response, stating that the connection between DOE's cited evidence and its policy changes was not readily apparent. The document also states that GAO limited its review to DOE's policies for reimbursing allowable contractor benefit costs, did not audit or verify data provided by DOE or its contractors for individual benefit plan activity and balances, did not audit or verify the amount or timing of payments by DOE to its contractors for allowable benefit costs or any other costs, and that the limited number of plan changes reviewed did not provide a basis for a conclusion on DOE's internal controls over benefit plan changes. GAO's review of DOE's actions to manage future costs and liabilities did not include identifying all actions DOE may have taken or evaluating the nature, extent, or effect of any such actions, and GAO neither verified the accuracy of the results of the benefit value studies nor evaluated contractors' conformance with DOE's requirements and guidance for performing such studies. In addition, information associating funded status amounts or benefit value scores with particular facilities or contractors was removed because DOE believes the information may be proprietary.
