about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, GAO-08-723, issued August 2008, examines the Health Resources and Services Administration's (HRSA) Health Center Program. It covers the extent to which federally designated medically underserved areas (MUAs) lacked health center sites in 2006, the services provided by sites in MUAs, how new access point grants awarded in 2007 changed the number of MUAs lacking sites, and HRSA's oversight of training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients and feedback to unsuccessful applicants. It makes four recommendations to the Administrator of HRSA.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report found that 47 percent of MUAs nationwide lacked a health center site in 2006, with wide variation across census regions and states. It could not determine the types of services provided by individual health center sites because HRSA does not collect and maintain readily available data on services at each site. New access point grants awarded in 2007 reduced the number of MUAs lacking a health center site by about 7 percent, leaving 43 percent of MUAs lacking a site in 2007, and wide geographic variation remained. The report also found that HRSA's oversight of cooperative agreement recipients is limited because it lacks standardized performance measures and is unlikely to meet its timeline for comprehensive on-site reviews. In addition, 38 percent of summary statements sent to unsuccessful applicants from fiscal years 2005 and 2007 contained unclear feedback.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In 2006, 1,600 of 3,421 MUAs nationwide, or 47 percent, lacked a health center site. By census region in 2006, 39 percent of MUAs in the Northeast, 45 percent in the South, 62 percent in the Midwest, and 32 percent in the West lacked a site. In 2007, 1,487 MUAs, or 43 percent, lacked a site, a decrease of 113 MUAs; regional percentages were 37 percent Northeast, 40 percent South, 60 percent Midwest, and 31 percent West. Decreases by region from 2006 to 2007 were: Northeast from 153 to 147, a decrease of 6 or 4 percent; Midwest from 641 to 617, a decrease of 24 or 4 percent; South from 651 to 574, a decrease of 77 or 12 percent; and West from 155 to 149, a decrease of 6 or 4 percent. In 2007, 202 new access point grants were awarded: 101, or 50 percent, to the South; 47, or 23 percent, to the West; 39, or 19 percent, to the Midwest; and 15, or 7 percent, to the Northeast. In the High Poverty County competition, 69 percent of awards went to applicants from the South, and nearly two-thirds of the 200 targeted counties were located in the South. In the open competition, 127 awards were made: 49, or 39 percent, to the South; 45, or 35 percent, to the West; 21, or 17 percent, to the Midwest; and 12, or 9 percent, to the Northeast. In 2006, approximately 1,000 health center grantees operated more than 6,000 health center sites and served more than 15 million people, and Health Center Program grants made up about 20 percent of all health center grantees' revenues. For fiscal year 2007, HRSA awarded nearly $53 million in cooperative agreements. In a random sample of 69 summary statements from fiscal years 2005 and 2007, 38 percent contained unclear feedback, and there were 41 distinct examples of unclear feedback. HRSA had conducted comprehensive on-site reviews for fewer than one-quarter of its training and TA cooperative agreement recipients that target assistance to new access point applicants since it implemented these reviews in 2004.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Administrator of HRSA take four actions: collect and maintain readily available data on the types of services provided at each health center site to improve the agency's ability to measure access to comprehensive primary care services in MUAs; develop and implement standardized performance measures for training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients that assist applicants, including a measure of the number of successful applicants a recipient assisted; reevaluate the policy of requiring comprehensive on-site reviews every 3 to 5 years and consider targeting available resources at cooperative agreement recipients most likely to benefit from such oversight; and identify and take appropriate action to ensure that the discussion of an applicant's strengths and weaknesses in all summary statements is clear.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle whether individuals in MUAs have access to the full range of comprehensive primary care services provided by health center sites; it states that this is unknown because HRSA does not collect and maintain data on services at individual sites. It also notes that it could not assess whether MUAs were sufficiently served. The report states its analysis may overestimate the number of MUAs that contained a health center site because it included whole zip codes associated with an MUA, and it assumed all health center sites operating in 2006 were still operating in 2007 because UDS data for 2007 were not yet available. It excluded grantees that served only medically underserved populations, covering 90 percent of Health Center Program grantees, and did not explicitly account for the proximity of health center sites located outside an MUA boundary. HRSA officials did not provide details on the standardized performance measures they said they were developing, so the report says it is unclear to what extent the proposed measures will allow HRSA to assess performance. HHS raised concerns that the percentage-of-MUAs indicator may be of limited utility and that collecting site-specific data would place a significant burden on grantees and raise administrative expenses.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Ranking Member, Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives, to support congressional oversight of the Health Center Program.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a June 20, 2008, U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-741) to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, House Committee on Veterans' Affairs. It compares the amount of Title IV federal student aid awarded to veteran students and nonveteran, independent students in their first year of full-time study, and it also examines how higher education institutions allocate Title IV aid among veterans and nonveterans and how federal agencies and schools provide veterans with information about Title IV aid. The scope covers veterans and active-duty personnel who served for three or more years and received Montgomery GI Bill Chapter 30 benefits; the report uses academic year 2005 to 2006 data for Pell Grants and Stafford Loans and 2003 to 2004 data for campus-based aid, and it excludes reservists.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own analysis found that veteran students received similar amounts of Title IV aid as nonveteran, independent students, but when Chapter 30 GI benefits were included, veterans received more total federal aid than nonveterans. Veterans received, on average, 6 percent less in Pell Grants than nonveterans in academic year 2005 to 2006, which the report attributes to veterans' higher average incomes rather than to Chapter 30 GI benefits, because those benefits are not counted as income for Pell Grant eligibility. Veterans received similar amounts of subsidized and unsubsidized Stafford Loans in 2005 to 2006 and similar amounts of campus-based aid in 2003 to 2004; the campus-based aid differences were not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level. Laws and regulations largely dictate how schools allocate Title IV aid, but five of the eight schools interviewed used their limited flexibility to allow veterans to be eligible for larger amounts of certain types of Title IV aid. Federal agencies and schools provide the same Title IV information to all students; two of the eight schools interviewed conducted targeted outreach to veterans at nearby military bases, and in 2007 the Department of Education began new efforts such as workshops for personnel separating from the military.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, the Department of Education provided $82 billion in Title IV aid to 11 million students and their families, and the Department of Veterans Affairs awarded about $2 billion in Chapter 30 GI benefits to more than 300,000 veteran students. Over the past decade, average college tuition and fees increased between 20 and 38 percent depending on the type of institution. In academic year 2005 to 2006, average Title IV aid amounts for first-year full-time students were: Pell Grant, $2,322 for veterans and $2,482 for nonveteran, independent students; subsidized Stafford Loan, $2,082 for veterans and $2,109 for nonveterans; unsubsidized Stafford Loan, $2,959 for veterans and $2,945 for nonveterans. Veterans received, on average, 6 percent less in Pell Grants than nonveterans in academic year 2005 to 2006. For campus-based aid in academic year 2003 to 2004, the estimated averages were $1,450 for veterans and $1,300 for nonveterans, amounts the report says were not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level. The average Chapter 30 GI benefit for veterans was $9,306 in academic year 2005 to 2006, based on $1,034 per month for a maximum of 36 months for veterans who completed an enlistment of three or more years and attended school full-time for an academic year of 9 months. Program award ranges in the report include: Pell Grants $400 to $4,050 in award year 2005 to 2006 and $400 to $4,310 in 2007 to 2008; subsidized Stafford Loans up to $2,625 in 2005 to 2006 and up to $3,500 in 2007 to 2008; unsubsidized Stafford Loans up to $6,625 for independent undergraduates in 2005 to 2006 and up to $7,500 in 2007 to 2008; Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants $100 to $4,000, except up to $4,400 for a study-abroad program, in both award years; Federal Perkins Loans up to $4,000 in both award years; and Federal Work-Study with no annual minimum or maximum award amounts up to the student's financial need in both award years. The report also gives an example from academic year 2005 to 2006 in which, at the 75th income percentile at public 2-year institutions, veterans had an average prior-year income of $38,550 and were eligible for a $1,600 Pell Grant, while nonveterans had an average prior-year income of $33,259 and were eligible for a $2,100 Pell Grant. Appendix III contains estimates for public 2-year, public 4-year, private 4-year, and proprietary institutions, with average costs of attendance of $11,692, $15,566, $31,916, and $22,931 respectively for academic year 2005 to 2006. The appendix notes also state that among dependent students who attended proprietary institutions in academic year 2003 to 2004, 20.3% received PLUS loans.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes no recommendations. It presents findings and concluding observations only.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that its findings on the eight schools cannot be generalized beyond those schools because they were selected as a nonprobability sample. It also states that it does not address how federal financial aid amounts reservists receive compare with other students, noting this may warrant further inquiry given the increasing number of reservists called to active duty in recent years and important differences in their receipt of GI benefits. The report notes that the most recent data available were for academic year 2005 to 2006 for Pell Grants and Stafford Loans and 2003 to 2004 for campus-based aid, and that students attending private 2-year schools were excluded due to lack of reliable data. It also cautions that unsubsidized Stafford Loan amounts for nonveteran, independent students assume that population has no other financial assistance such as outside scholarships, and that individual veterans may be eligible for more Title IV aid but received, on average, similar amounts, with contributing factors including income and students' decisions not to take loans for which they were eligible. The report notes differing views on whether veterans should have advantages in receiving Title IV aid and that some veterans may be unaware or confused about Title IV aid or mistakenly think they are not eligible because of Chapter 30 GI benefits.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees, GAO-08-773, issued September 10, 2008. It assesses the Department of Defense's implementation of the National Security Personnel System (NSPS), focusing on two questions: the extent to which DOD has implemented accountability mechanisms and internal safeguards for fairness, effectiveness, and credibility of the NSPS performance management system, and how DOD civilian personnel perceive NSPS and what actions DOD has taken to address those perceptions. It covers DOD and the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Fourth Estate components, using site visits, interviews, DOD employee surveys, and discussion groups.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's main finding is that DOD has taken some steps to implement internal safeguards for NSPS, but implementation of three safeguards could be improved immediately: predecisional internal safeguards, reasonable transparency over final rating results, and meaningful distinctions in employee performance. DOD does not require a third-party predecisional analysis of rating results for anomalies; some installations do not publish rating and share distributions; and guidance that most employees should be rated '3' may discourage use of all rating categories. The report also finds that NSPS employees were more positive than other DOD employees on some performance-management items, but employees with the most NSPS experience showed declining attitudes, and DOD has no action plan to address generally negative employee perceptions. The report's discussion groups identified concerns about morale, time burden, writing skills influencing ratings, lack of transparency of pay pool panels, and rapid implementation.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of May 2008, 182,630 DOD civilian employees had been phased into NSPS, with about 273,000 employees remaining to be phased in. In the design phase, DOD received over 58,000 comments on proposed rules, and about 71,000 employees, about 14 percent, responded to a Web-based questionnaire. Training figures in the report are 10 hours for transitioning employees, 18 hours of basic and 24 hours of pay pool panel training for managers and supervisors, 10 hours for employees, and 26 or more hours for human resource practitioners. DOD's November 2005 cost estimate to implement NSPS for fiscal years 2005 through 2008 was $158 million; the revised estimate for fiscal years 2009 through 2011 is approximately $143 million. In the May 2007 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 43 percent of NSPS employees, as stated in the report's results-in-brief, and an estimated 25 percent of all other DOD employees said pay raises depend on how well employees perform their jobs; separately, the report states an estimated 40 percent of all NSPS employees and 43 percent of spiral 1.1 employees agreed with that statement. The estimated percentage of spiral 1.1 employees who agreed that their performance appraisal was a fair reflection of performance declined from 67 percent in May 2006 to 52 percent in May 2007, and the percentage who believed NSPS would have a positive effect on DOD's personnel practices dropped from 40 percent in May 2006 to 23 percent in May 2007. The report's table 2 gives DOD-wide rating category percentages of 0.2 percent for category 1, 1.6 percent for category 2, 57.0 percent for category 3, 36.1 percent for category 4, and 5.1 percent for category 5.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that DOD improve implementation of three safeguards by requiring a third party to perform predecisional demographic and other analysis as appropriate for pay pools, requiring overall final rating results to be published, and encouraging pay pools and supervisors to use all categories of ratings as appropriate. The report also recommends that DOD develop and implement a specific action plan to address employee perceptions of NSPS ascertained from DOD's surveys and employee focus groups, including actions to mitigate employee concerns such as the potential influence of writing skills on panels' assessments of employee ratings or other issues consistently identified by employees or supervisors.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that its discussion-group information is not generalizable to the entire population of DOD civilians. It says GAO was unable to determine whether the final rating distributions it reviewed were meaningful because GAO did not have specific knowledge of employees' performance within those pay pools. It also notes that DOD's surveys were generally conducted in accordance with standard research practices but had some areas that could be improved. The report says it does not know what the overall trend in employee attitudes is or whether the negative movement will continue in future years, and that trends can be identified only after employees have had more time under NSPS and additional surveys are administered. The report also notes that DOD has not developed a new timeline for phasing in the remaining approximately 273,000 employees.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report to congressional requesters assessing the Department of Homeland Security's handling of lessons learned from its first Cyber Storm cyber attack simulation exercise. It covers the lessons DHS identified from Cyber Storm I, the status of DHS's corrective activities, and key participants' views of the second Cyber Storm exercise.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: DHS identified eight lessons from Cyber Storm I, involving interagency coordination groups; contingency planning, risk assessment, and roles and responsibilities; integration of incidents across infrastructures; access to information; coordination of response activities; strategic communications and public relations; processes, tools, and technology; and the exercise program. DHS identified 66 activities to address these lessons; as of June 2008, 42 were completed, 1 was reported as completed but not validated, 16 were ongoing, and 7 were planned for the future. DHS had not identified completion dates for activities reported as ongoing. Cyber Storm II participants observed progress and continued challenges in areas including roles and responsibilities, public relations, communications, exercise infrastructure, and handling of classified information, and many of these challenges were similar to those identified during Cyber Storm I. GAO concluded that until DHS schedules and completes its remaining corrective activities, it risks wasting resources on subsequent exercises that repeat the lessons learned in 2006. DHS concurred with GAO's recommendation and reported completing additional items after the draft report, raising the completion percentage to over 70 percent, but GAO did not modify the activity statuses because DHS had not yet provided sufficient evidence.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Cyber Storm I was conducted in February 2006 at a cost of about $3.7 million, with eight federal departments and three agencies, three states, four foreign countries, 11 information technology companies, 7 electric companies, 1 banking and finance company, 2 airlines, and over 100 public and private agencies, associations, and corporations. Cyber Storm II was conducted in March 2008 at a cost of about $6.4 million, involving 18 federal agencies, 9 states, 10 information sharing and analysis centers, 5 foreign countries, and over 40 industry representatives from the private sector. DHS identified 66 activities to address the eight lessons; as of June 2008, 42 were reported and validated as completed, 1 was reported as completed but not validated due to insufficient evidence, 16 were ongoing, and 7 were planned for the future. DHS listed 121 activities to address lessons 1 through 8, of which 55 repeat a prior activity. The per-lesson activity counts were: interagency coordination groups, 32 activities with 24 completed and 8 ongoing or planned; contingency planning, risk assessment, and roles and responsibilities, 15 activities with 8 completed and 7 ongoing or planned; integration of incidents across infrastructures, 16 activities with 9 completed and 7 ongoing or planned; access to information, 15 activities with 8 completed and 7 ongoing or planned; coordination of response activities, 15 activities with 11 completed and 4 ongoing or planned; strategic communications and public relations, 5 activities with 1 completed and 4 ongoing or planned; processes, tools, and technology, 12 activities with 8 completed and 4 ongoing or planned; and the exercise program, 11 activities with 9 completed and 2 ongoing or planned. DHS had completed over 60 percent of the 66 activities at the time the report was drafted, and DHS reported that after the draft report it completed additional items, raising the percentage to over 70 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes one recommendation for executive action: the Secretary of Homeland Security should direct the Assistant Secretary for Cybersecurity and Communications to ensure the scheduling and completion of the corrective actions addressing lessons learned during Cyber Storm I before conducting the next Cyber Storm exercise. DHS concurred with the recommendation and stated it will continue to address actions related to Cyber Storm I findings. The report also notes that federal policy and DHS exercise program guidance require corrective actions to be identified, tracked, and given a time frame for implementation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle completion dates for DHS's remaining corrective activities: DHS identified completion dates for its planned activities but not for activities reported as ongoing. DHS stated that end dates are not applicable for many of the remaining corrective actions because they are either dependent upon outside stakeholder actions or are ongoing or long-term activities being addressed incrementally, while GAO found that most of the remaining activities are finite and could be associated with a time frame. The document also notes that DHS plans to issue a report on what it learned from Cyber Storm II by the end of 2008, and that the observations of Cyber Storm II participants are not intended to be generalized to other exercise participants. GAO did not modify the status of activities DHS said it completed after the draft report because DHS had not yet provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate completion.

audience.text: This report is for congressional requesters, specifically the Chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security and the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Emerging Threats, Cybersecurity, and Science and Technology, to support congressional oversight of DHS's cybersecurity exercise program.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: GAO-08-854, issued June 26, 2008, is a 36-page U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees on the Defense Production Act of 1950. It examines the extent to which agencies use DPA authorities and assesses agencies' response to reporting requirements on the economic impact of foreign offsets, focusing on use since the 2003 reauthorization in defense, energy, domestic emergency and disaster response and recovery, and critical infrastructure. Its main conclusion is that agencies lack policies and guidance for use of key DPA authorities.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's own findings are that the Department of Defense is the primary user of DPA authorities, routinely placing priority ratings on almost all of its contracts for industrial resources, about 300,000 annually, while civilian agency use has been limited. Civilian agencies generally have not used Title I priorities and allocations authority and, unlike DOD, would decide on a case-by-case basis after a delivery problem has been identified, potentially delaying critical products in emergencies. Civilian agencies responsible for civil transportation, health resources, and food and agriculture resources have not developed and implemented policies or guidance for Title I; HHS and USDA are beginning to develop regulations, while DOT has not yet begun. Title III authority has been used almost exclusively for defense needs, with DOD generally the sole user, and events that would trigger some Title VII authorities, such as the National Defense Executive Reserve and voluntary agreements, have not occurred. On foreign offsets, agencies have taken steps toward fulfilling reporting requirements, but Commerce's data limits analysis, the interagency team has reached consensus that adverse effects exist but not on best practices, and the National Commission on Offsets never produced its final report.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is GAO-08-854, 36 pages, issued June 26, 2008. DOD places priority ratings on approximately 300,000 contracts annually. DHS has authorized or endorsed the use of priority ratings 15 times since 2003, with over half in support of critical infrastructure protection and restoration. Commerce has taken approximately 180 Special Priorities Assistance actions since late 2003. The DPA offset reporting regulation applies to offset agreements exceeding $5 million in value. Commerce's annual offset report did not include the potential effects of nearly $1 billion of technology transfer, training, and overseas investment offset transactions, representing nearly 24 percent of average annual offset transactions. The 2004 subcontractor survey had a response rate of less than 40 percent; documentation was requested for only two weapon systems from each of 13 U.S. prime contractors out of nearly 700 weapon systems and components contracts for the 5-year period 1998 through 2002. Currently, 84 percent of the value of export contracts involving offsets submitted by prime contractors is for the aerospace industry. The National Commission on Offsets produced an interim report in 2001 and never produced its final report. Figure 1's fiscal-year Title III project counts, DOD-initiated and congressionally requested respectively, are: 2002, 1 and 0; 2003, 1 and 0; 2004, 0 and 2; 2005, 5 and 3; 2006, 1 and 6; 2007, 2 and 4; 2008, 0 and 7. DOD proposed statutory changes including increasing the Title III limit from $50,000,000 to $200,000,000 before specific authorization in law is required, reducing the required waiting period for awarding contracts from 60 to 30 days, and changing Congressional notification from the annual budget cycle, which creates a waiting period of up to one year. DHS reported that it could take 21 to 50 days to establish a voluntary agreement following a disaster. DOT used a priority rating to support procurement of approximately 1,800 Explosives Detection Systems machines for U.S. airports, required to be installed by December 31, 2002. Title III project funds listed in Table 2 are $163.91 million for radiation-hardened microelectronics, $67.10 million for beryllium, $20.41 million for titanium metal matrix composites, $16.42 million for silicon carbide MMICs, $16.20 million for lithium ion batteries, $14.62 million for high temperature flexible aerogel, $13.96 million for integrated advanced composite fiber placement, $13.73 million for POSS nanotechnology, $11.44 million for high performance thermal batteries, $9.87 million for radiation-hardened cryogenic read out integrated circuits, $9.18 million for next-generation radiation-hardened microprocessors, $9.14 million for thin silicon-on-insulator wafers, $8.37 million for reactive plastic CO2 absorbent, $7.95 million for miniature compressors, $5.42 million for ALD hermetic coatings, $5.34 million for ALON and spinel optical ceramics, $5.30 million for TWT amplifiers for space, $4.00 million for YBCO superconductors, $3.38 million for photovoltaic solar cell encapsulant, $3.09 million for silicon powder and ceramic armor, $2.84 million for military lens systems, $2.43 million for methanol fuel cell components, $1.91 million for coal based carbon foam, $1.06 million for amplifying fluorescent polymer IED detection devices, $0.88 million for continuous filament boron fiber, $31.38 million for projects with contracts not yet awarded, and a total of $449.3 million.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Commerce, develop and implement a system for using the priorities and allocations authority for food and agriculture resources, health resources, and civil transportation, respectively. It also recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, and Transportation consider, in advance of an emergency, approving programs and placing priority ratings on contracts for items likely to be needed in an emergency. In addition, it recommends that the Secretary of Commerce update regulations to, for example, request more specific industry information from prime contractors to improve the assessment of the economic effects of offsets. USDA generally concurred with the findings and recommendations, and HHS and DOT indicated in technical comments that they will implement the recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it does not settle the economic effect of offsets, because available reports do not provide a basis for fully evaluating that effect. The interagency team has reached consensus that adverse effects exist but not on best practices to address them; participants identified challenges including a lack of agreement on terminology and differences in views, and participating nations noted that producing a preliminary statement of best practices will be difficult and time-consuming. The National Commission on Offsets' final report and recommendations were never produced. The Bureau of Industry and Security's review of data and methodology is ongoing, with the outcome anticipated in the next annual report, but changes to the regulation would not affect data collection for that report. The report also leaves open how quickly civilian agencies will complete their systems: HHS has no timeline for completing regulations, DOT has not yet begun the process, DHS is still establishing policies and procedures, and FEMA is assessing the need for its National Defense Executive Reserve.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees listed in the letter — the Senate and House Armed Services Committees, the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the House Committee on Financial Services — to support congressional oversight of Defense Production Act use and offset reporting.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-860, issued July 31, 2008) on the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership (TSCTP), the primary U.S. counterterrorism policy vehicle in northwestern Africa. It covers TSCTP's operations in nine partner countries—Chad, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, Nigeria, and Senegal—and examines (1) how TSCTP funds were distributed in fiscal years 2005 through 2008 and what kinds of activities were supported, and (2) how the program was implemented, including whether it was guided by a comprehensive, integrated strategy. The report is based on a performance audit conducted from July 2007 to July 2008, including site visits to Morocco, Mali, and Mauritania.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The GAO's own findings are that the key agencies—State, USAID, and DOD—distributed most TSCTP funds to Sahel countries and supported diplomacy, development assistance, and military activities. The GAO found that implementation was hampered by the lack of a comprehensive, integrated strategy; by disagreements between State and DOD over whether State has authority over DOD personnel temporarily assigned to TSCTP activities in partner countries; by fluctuation in funding that caused USAID to suspend a peace-building program in Mali; and by the lack of common mechanisms for measuring outcomes. State and USAID concurred with the findings and recommendations, and DOD partially concurred.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that since the program's inception, key agencies' obligations and commitments for TSCTP amounted to about $353 million. For 2005 through 2007, agencies obligated about $230 million; for 2008, commitments were approximately $123 million. About 74 percent of the approximately $230 million obligated in 2005 through 2007 went to the Sahel countries (Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger), about 3 percent to the Maghreb countries (Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia), about 8 percent to the sub-Saharan countries (Nigeria and Senegal), and the remaining 15 percent to regional assistance. For 2008, as of June 2008, the agencies expected to distribute about 49 percent to the Sahel, 21 percent to the Maghreb, 13 percent to the sub-Saharan countries, and 17 percent for regional assistance. An additional $147 million was obligated for program support costs for all TSCTP partner countries. By fiscal year and agency, DOD and State/USAID obligations and commitments were: 2005, $7 million DOD and $18 million State/USAID; 2006, $39 million and $10 million; 2007, $118 million and $37 million; 2008, $92 million and $31 million. By country and period, the report lists: Chad, 2005-2007, $23 million; 2008, $9 million; total $32 million. Mali, $31 million; $6 million; $37 million. Mauritania, $18 million; $6 million; $24 million. Niger, $37 million; $7 million; $44 million. Algeria, $1 million; $6 million; $7 million. Morocco, $3 million; $6 million; $9 million. Tunisia, 0; $1 million; $1 million. Senegal, $9 million; $3 million; $12 million. Nigeria, $3 million; $5 million; $8 million. Regional, $22 million; $10 million; $30 million. Figure 9 gives exact State and USAID obligations by country and fiscal year: Chad, $2,780,000 in 2005, $2,990,000 in 2006, $2,895,000 in 2007; Mali, $2,330,000, $550,000, $13,570,000; Mauritania, $2,620,000, $58,000, $6,200,000; Niger, $3,220,000, $4,340,000, $5,372,000; Algeria, $417,876, 0, 0; Morocco, $1,550,000, $463,381, $382,423; Tunisia, 0, $32,836, 0; Nigeria, 0, 0, $1,260,000; Senegal, $397,000, $1,160,000, $3,970,000; regional, $5,000,000, 0, $3,650,000. The report also states that USAID was working with the United Nations Development Program to reintegrate more than 3,000 ex-rebel fighters in Niger.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The GAO recommends that the Secretary of State work through the Director of Foreign Assistance, who serves concurrently as USAID Administrator, to develop a comprehensive strategy for the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership in conjunction with the Secretaries of Defense and the Treasury, the U.S. Attorney General, and the heads of any other participating agencies. The strategy should include clear goals, objectives, and milestones, including output and outcome indicators, and identify resources needed to achieve the program's goals. The GAO also recommends that the Secretaries of State and Defense develop and issue joint guidance with regard to DOD personnel temporarily assigned to conduct TSCTP activities in the partner countries.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that as of June 2008 no comprehensive, integrated strategy had been developed, despite it being identified as a priority at annual TSCTP conferences, and that none of the nine partner countries' DOD country action plans had been approved by the ambassadors. It states that disagreements between State and DOD over authority over DOD personnel could not be resolved at the country level and required higher-level guidance or intervention. The document also states that the agencies had few common mechanisms for measuring outcomes, that agency officials noted the difficulty of measuring how certain activities, such as building wells or providing radios, contribute to TSCTP goals, and that the agencies were working to develop common indicators. It notes data limitations because there is no central repository for TSCTP funds and figures were rounded to the nearest millions of dollars, although it concludes the data were sufficiently reliable for the report's objectives. It also states that a classified annex to the report was planned.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Ranking Member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and it supports congressional oversight, policy, and funding decisions regarding U.S. counterterrorism assistance in northwestern Africa.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees, issued August 22, 2008, on the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB). It examines how CSB has responded to GAO and inspector general recommendations concerning its investigative gap, data quality problems, human capital problems, and accountability and management problems, and it assesses the merits of the current oversight approach using an existing inspector general office and alternative oversight approaches. The review was a performance audit conducted from October 2007 to May 2008 in response to a mandate in the Joint Explanatory Statement accompanying the fiscal year 2008 Consolidated Appropriations Act.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: CSB has implemented some GAO and IG recommendations since GAO last reported in July 2000, but it has not fully addressed several critical recommendations, and problems in governance, management, and oversight persist. The investigative gap persists: CSB continues to fall short of its statutory mandate by not investigating all accidental releases that result, or have the potential to result, in a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage, and it has not developed a long-term plan for reporting to Congress on the scope and magnitude of the gap. Data quality problems continue because CSB has not published the required data-reporting regulation and lacks a long-term strategy to improve quality controls, leaving its accident-screening database somewhat inaccurate and incomplete. Human capital problems persist because CSB lacks a comprehensive human capital plan, has difficulty attracting and retaining investigators, and more employees left than were hired in fiscal years 2006 and 2007. Accountability and management problems continue because CSB operates without a permanent chief operating officer and lacks a permanent senior executive to establish performance goals and hold program managers accountable. GAO concludes that independent oversight from an existing inspector general remains the most effective way to help CSB address its continuing problems, provided the arrangement is made permanent and funding is provided, and that after 10 years of operation CSB continues to operate in noncompliance with its statutory mandates.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: CSB is to be managed by a five-member board, and currently the board has one vacancy. CSB received an appropriation of $9.4 million for fiscal year 2008 and had 39 staff as of January 30, 2008. CSB reported to Congress that it received notification of approximately 900 chemical accidents in calendar year 2007, and that 31 of these accidents were serious or even fatal events that warranted the commitment of CSB investigators. Since fiscal year 2001, three inspectors general have made 32 recommendations to CSB. Using fiscal year 2002 data, the DHS IG reported in fiscal year 2004 that CSB deployed to 4 of 294 accidents that met statutory criteria for investigation. In fiscal year 2007, CSB received notifications of 920 chemical accidents; approximately 35 of these accidents included at least one fatality, and CSB investigated 1. CSB investigated less than 1 percent, or 5 of 920, of the accidents of which it was notified in fiscal year 2007. In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, CSB recorded 822 and 920 total accidents in its screening database, deployed to 9 and 8 accidents, investigated 6 and 5 accidents, recorded 38 and 35 accidents with fatalities, and investigated 5 and 1 accidents with fatalities. GAO found at least five accidents, about 6 percent of the cases reviewed, where fatalities were not correctly recorded, and seven accidents, about 4 percent of the cases reviewed, where data on injuries were missing. In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, 7 noninvestigative staff and 4 investigators were hired, while 9 noninvestigative staff and 5 investigators left; 3 of the 5 investigators who left were senior investigators with 5 to 7 years of experience. Of the investigators hired, 1 was a senior investigator at GS-13 and 3 were intern investigators at GS-7, along with 7 other staff. Two of four intern investigators hired in fiscal years 2004 and 2005 left CSB, and one transferred to another office. CSB has not paid a retention bonus to any employee since September 2002. In fiscal year 2006, CSB reprogrammed compensation funds of $627,891 to other priorities, and in fiscal year 2007 it reprogrammed compensation funds of $407,383 to similar purchases. NTSB's budget is approximately 8 times CSB's budget, and NTSB investigates 250 times as many accidents. In fiscal year 2006, CSB started 6 investigations with a budget of $9.1 million, while NTSB started 1,521 aviation investigations with a budget of $75.9 million; the 1,521 figure is aviation accident investigations only, and NTSB completed 19 nonaviation accident investigations in fiscal year 2006. CSB requested $10.6 million and 47 staff for fiscal year 2009 and requested $12.5 million and 60 staff in fiscal year 2000. Prior appropriations and staff levels were $9.4 million and 39 staff for fiscal year 2008, $9.2 million and 41 staff for fiscal year 2006, $8.2 million and 40 staff for fiscal year 2004, and $8.0 million and 27 staff for fiscal year 2000. CSB is one of 54 federal entities defined in the Inspector General Act of 1978 for which the act did not provide an inspector general. CSB noted that it currently obtains its financial and information security audits for about $60,000 a year.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the chairman of the Chemical Safety Board develop a plan to address the investigative gap and request the necessary resources from Congress to meet CSB's statutory mandate or seek an amendment to its statutory mandate; consider using the work of other entities, such as government agencies, companies, and contractors, to a greater extent to maximize the board's limited resources; improve the quality of its accident-screening database by better controlling data entry and periodically sampling accident data to evaluate their consistency and completeness; publish a regulation requiring facilities to report all chemical accidents, as required by law, to better inform the agency of important details about accidents that it may not receive from current sources; consider reinstating the position of chief operating officer, with delegations of responsibility for establishing performance goals, holding program managers accountable for meeting those goals, and demonstrating improvement in the agency's ability to meet its statutory mandates over time; and use the Strategic Management of Human Capital portion of the President's Management Agenda to provide criteria for developing a comprehensive human capital plan, with input from investigators, that includes specific objectives and performance measures. The document also proposes matters for congressional consideration: Congress may wish to consider amending CSB's authorizing statute or the Inspector General Act of 1978 to permanently give EPA's Inspector General the authority to serve as the oversight body for the agency, and Congress may wish to consider providing the EPA Inspector General with appropriations and staff allocations specifically for the audit function of CSB via a direct line in the EPA appropriation. The document notes that CSB generally concurred with four of the six recommendations and disagreed with two, and disagreed with both matters for congressional consideration.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that GAO did not evaluate the quality of CSB's investigative products issued to date, or the quality and effectiveness of its reports, recommendations, and promotion of preventive actions, because those evaluations were outside the scope of the mandate and not relevant to the findings and conclusions. It also did not conduct a detailed evaluation of the oversight arrangements for the other 53 federal entities for comparison with CSB. The document notes that the accident-screening database is sufficiently reliable for making broad estimates of the total number of accidents and accidents with fatalities, but its limitations include the lack of quality controls to ensure that data are accurate and complete, especially with respect to fatalities, and that totals may be underestimated. An unresolved disagreement is whether CSB's authorizing statute requires investigation of every chemical accident involving a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage: CSB stated it has not construed the statute that way, while GAO continues to believe the law is clear and that a plan to address the investigative gap is still necessary. CSB said it would work with Congress to clarify the issue and, if appropriate, seek an amendment to its authorizing statute. The document also records CSB's disagreements with GAO's recommendation to publish a reporting regulation, with both matters for congressional consideration, and with GAO's view that using the EPA Inspector General does not pose a risk to CSB's independent evaluation of chemical accidents; GAO maintained its positions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to Congressional requesters assessing the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's (PBGC) contracting function. It covers the role of contracting in PBGC's mission, steps taken to improve its acquisition infrastructure and strategic approach, and steps taken to improve contract oversight to ensure accountability. It includes GAO's conclusions and recommendations for executive action.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: PBGC relies heavily on contractors to address unpredictable workloads: its current workforce is roughly two-thirds contractor employees and one-third federal employees. Contract spending and use of contract employees increased steadily from fiscal years 2000 through 2007, and growth in contract employees outpaced hiring of federal employees. PBGC is taking steps to improve its acquisition infrastructure, but its Procurement Department is not yet part of PBGC's strategic decision-making process and a strategic approach to contracting has not yet been developed. PBGC has made improvements to contractor oversight since GAO's last report, including new monitoring activities, improved oversight of major contracts, and comprehensive procedures, but most current contracts still lack performance incentives and methods to hold contractors accountable. PBGC recently began awarding more performance-based contracts, which may present implementation challenges.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, roughly 611,000 beneficiaries received over $4.1 billion in benefit payments. PBGC insured pensions for more than 44 million workers in over 30,000 employer-sponsored defined benefit plans. As of September 2007, PBGC showed an accumulated deficit of $14 billion for its single-employer program. PBGC's budget increased from $165 million in fiscal year 2000 to $398 million in fiscal year 2007, and contract spending increased from $122 million in fiscal year 2000 to $297 million in fiscal year 2007; contracting represented 71 percent of PBGC's appropriated budget during this period. PBGC had 791 contract employees in fiscal year 2000 and over 1,500 in fiscal year 2007, while federal employees increased from 763 in fiscal year 2000 to 811 in fiscal year 2007. Contract employees peaked at 1,768 in fiscal year 2006 and fell to 1,502 in fiscal year 2007. PBGC manages $68 billion of assets. PBGC to date has awarded less than $150 million in service contract dollars in fiscal year 2008, and only six of its contracts currently are performance based, representing a yearly cost of approximately $30 million. Only 2 of 12 staff in the contract specialist series were certified in contracting as of February 2007; by January 2008, 9 of the 12 staff had been certified.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of PBGC revise its strategic plan and, in drafting the corporation's human capital strategic plan, reflect the importance of contracting and PBGC's use of contractors, project its vision of future contractor use, and better link staffing and contracting decisions at the corporate level. Specifically, it recommends including the Procurement Department in agency-wide strategic planning; ensuring the Procurement Director sits on the Operations Integration Board, the Budget and Planning Integration Team, and the Capital Planning for Information Technology Team; broadening the May 2007 staffing study to include acquisition-related positions outside the Procurement Department; including detailed plans for how contract support will be obtained in the human capital plan; assessing contract information to support strategic acquisition management decisions; and developing metrics for the annual performance plan that document how the acquisition function supports PBGC's missions and goals. To improve contract management as PBGC implements performance-based contracting, the report recommends providing comprehensive training on performance-based contracting for Procurement Department staff, managers, and acquisition-related workforce; developing practices to ensure accountability for Procurement Department staff carrying out contract monitoring responsibilities; and ensuring future contracts measure performance in terms of outcomes, provide incentives for desired outcomes, and ensure payment of award fees only for excellent performance.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is still too early to tell what the effect of the new policies will be, and that GAO did not conduct an independent assessment of PBGC's May 2007 staffing study to validate its results. It notes that PBGC may face challenges similar to those faced by other government agencies during implementation of performance-based contracting, and that the American Customer Service Index is not completely effective as an incentive mechanism because it does not report results for individual contractors. It also notes that not all COTR site visits are being conducted as anticipated, with only one to two being conducted per office each year, and that PBGC does not foresee large plan terminations and bankruptcies coming in 2008 or 2009 but is monitoring a few plans that could have significant impact.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is for Congressional requesters—specifically the Chairmen and Ranking Members of the Senate Committee on Finance and the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions—to support their oversight of PBGC's contracting activities.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to congressional requesters examining whether the Department of Defense and the military services are acquiring tactical radios in a cost-efficient and effective manner and whether DOD has developed a strategy to balance near- and long-term requirements, address capability gaps, and determine funding needs. It focuses on how planned investments in key tactical radio systems changed over fiscal years 2003-2007, why those changes occurred, and the challenges facing the services in planning future tactical radio investments, particularly balancing investment between legacy radios and the Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS).

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that DOD's tactical radio investments shifted dramatically in size and composition: planned spending of about $3.2 billion over fiscal years 2003-2007 for JTRS and Army and Marine Corps legacy radios became actual spending of about $8.3 billion, with about $5.7 billion spent on legacy radios and $2.5 billion on JTRS development, and no JTRS networking radios produced or fielded during that time. The change was due primarily to delays in JTRS development and production and to urgent demands for additional legacy radios from combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, force modernization, and a change in concept of operations requiring more radios per unit. Supplemental funding supplied most of the additional funds, and the waiver/notification process was not effective in tracking legacy radio investments. Looking ahead, DOD faces challenges completing JTRS development, managing investments within tighter fiscal constraints, and developing a fielding strategy, and DOD does not have a strategy for balancing future tactical radio investments.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports that DOD spent an estimated $12 billion on development and production of tactical radios over the last 5 years, comparable to estimated investments of $10.4 billion in the Army's Future Combat Systems and $10.8 billion in the Navy's Virginia Class submarines during the same period. For fiscal years 2003-2007, DOD planned to invest close to $3 billion in JTRS—about $1 billion to develop and test and $2 billion to start procuring—while the Army and Marine Corps planned to spend only about $235 million on legacy radios. Compared with the $3.2 billion slated to be spent on JTRS and the Army and Marine Corps legacy radios, about $8.3 billion was actually spent, of which about $5.7 billion was spent on legacy radios and $2.5 billion on JTRS development. Supplemental funding supplied an estimated $5.5 billion of the additional funds, or about 90 percent—$5.5 billion out of $6.1 billion—of the funding the Army and Marine Corps received to procure legacy radios between 2003 and 2007. The Army spent approximately $4.1 billion on legacy radios, including $2.3 billion on SINCGARS and $1.8 billion on handheld and manpack radios, and the Marine Corps spent $1.6 billion. The estimated cost to develop JTRS increased from about $3.5 billion to almost $6 billion through fiscal year 2011. A legacy vehicle radio costs about $20,000, while its JTRS replacement is estimated to cost up to 10 times more; the average cost of the 4-channel vehicular JTRS Ground Mobile Radio is about $220,000, and the average unit cost of the 2-channel airborne JTRS radio is about $480,000, compared to a latest-generation AN/ARC-210 cost of about $80,000. The estimated cost to retrofit and fully integrate JTRS networking capabilities into four Naval aircraft is about $868 million. The Army's authorized acquisition objective for SINCGARS rose from 232,411 units in fiscal year 2002 to 526,192 in fiscal year 2007, and the Army bought 244,780 SINCGARS between 2003 and 2007; the Army estimated it would need an additional 66,166 SINCGARS receiver/transmitter units for modularity. A typical Marine Corps rifle company was equipped with 9 tactical radios before the war in Iraq and is now equipped with about 225. JTRS procurement quantities were reduced from initial approved quantities of 108,086 Ground Mobile Radios to 86,512; from 328,514 Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit radios to 95,551; and from a total of 436,600 to 193,103. Other reported figures include the Army's $310 million estimated spending between 2005 and 2013 for an alternate helicopter radio, the Navy's approximately $50 million modernization plan for the AN/ARC-210, the $3.3 billion fiscal year 2008 supplemental request, the $1.7 billion Army overstatement for SINCGARS funding, the Army's request for 170,756 more SINCGARS when only 56,000 were needed, the 3.8-pound weight limit for a 2-channel handheld JTRS radio, and the preliminary $2,000 unit cost estimate for the JTRS 'Rifleman' Radio versus $8,700 for the small form factor 'C' radio.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Defense develop a comprehensive strategy and implementation plan for making sound tactical radio investment decisions that is based on operational architectures defining battlefield communications and networking functions, assesses and prioritizes near- and long-term capabilities and requirements, sets bounds for committed funding, lays out an effective migration and fielding plan, and identifies contingencies in case of further JTRS problems and delays. It also recommends that the Secretary of Defense reinvigorate the tactical radio notification/waiver process to provide department-wide insight into continued procurement of legacy and interim radios, with clear guidance and procedures developed and communicated. The document reports that DOD agreed with both recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the JTRS program must still overcome technology hurdles, size and power constraints, and security architecture issues, and that whether these technical challenges can be overcome will not be known until major test and evaluation events are conducted in the next few years. It notes that DOD's joint migration plan from October 2003 has not been updated, the services' input for a new fielding plan has not been linked to operational architectures and has lacked detail on requirements and funding priorities, and a comprehensive plan that balances needs with resources, targets JTRS investments, identifies contingencies, and provides central direction is still lacking. The document also notes that GAO was unable to obtain tactical radio investment plans or actual procurement information from the Navy or Air Force because those services do not centrally procure radios.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Air and Land Forces, House Committee on Armed Services, to support congressional oversight and decisions regarding DOD's management and acquisition of tactical radio systems.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued July 16, 2008, responds to a congressional mandate and examines state and local practices in allocating and using four federal tax incentives created or expanded by the Gulf Opportunity Zone Act of 2005: $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bond authority, $330 million in low-income housing tax credits, $350 million in GO Zone tax credit bonds, and $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds. It covers Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas, describing the states' allocation processes, compliance and fraud-prevention practices, and how much of the incentives had been used and for what purposes as of mid-June 2008 for bonds and April 2008 for housing tax credits.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that the GO Zone Act gave state governments responsibility for allocating four federal tax incentives between 2006 and 2010. Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi generally allocated the GO Zone bond provisions on a first-come, first-served basis, with some variation in their processes, while all five eligible states used existing procedures to award GO Zone low-income housing tax credits. The states generally did not consistently target private activity bond allocations to the most damaged areas, although Louisiana later set aside some remaining authority for the most damaged parishes. State officials said they rely on bond counsel opinions to ensure eligibility and on required IRS information returns for compliance. As of mid-June 2008, the three eligible states had allocated about 87 percent of the $14.9 billion in private activity bond authority, but bonds had been issued for only about 44 percent of the total authority. As of April 2008, the five states had awarded 95 percent of the $330 million in LIHTCs, but few planned units were in service. Louisiana and Mississippi exhausted their $300 million combined tax credit bond authority, while Alabama did not issue tax credit bonds. The three states used 16 percent of their advance refunding authority. State officials identified challenges including reduced credit availability, declining tax credit values, difficulty identifying eligible debt, and educating investors about tax credit bonds. No cases of fraud, waste, or abuse were identified, though officials indicated some projects that may have been viable without tax-exempt financing received bond authority.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports that the 2005 hurricanes left more than 1,500 people dead, with estimated capital losses of $70 billion to more than $150 billion. Federal rebuilding assistance included $10.4 billion from FEMA's Public Assistance program as of April 2008 and $19.7 billion from HUD's CDBG program as of May 2008. The GO Zone Act incentives were projected to reduce federal revenue by about $9 billion from 2006 to 2015, with the four state-allocated incentives accounting for about 40 percent, or $3.5 billion, of that cost. Allocation authority was $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bonds (Alabama $2,174 million, Louisiana $7,840 million, Mississippi $4,921 million; total $14,935 million); $330 million in LIHTCs (Alabama $47 million, Louisiana $170 million, Mississippi $106 million; total $323 million, plus $3.5 million each for Florida and Texas in 2006); $350 million in GO Zone tax credit bonds (Alabama $50 million, Louisiana $200 million, Mississippi $100 million); and $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds (Alabama $1,125 million, Louisiana $4,500 million, Mississippi $2,250 million; total $7,875 million). The projected revenue reductions were about $1.6 billion for private activity bonds, $1.1 billion for LIHTCs, $57 million for tax credit bonds, and $741 million for advance refundings. In 2008, state volume caps for tax-exempt private activity bonds were about $393 million for Alabama, $365 million for Louisiana, and $262 million for Mississippi. The regular LIHTC allocation in 2006 was $1.90 per capita, while the GO Zone LIHTC allocation was $18.00 times each state's prehurricane GO Zone population. Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi received about $27 million, $26 million, and $17 million from regular LIHTC allocations for 2006 through 2008, respectively; their GO Zone LIHTC authority was about 75 percent, 567 percent, and 523 percent greater than that regular authority. GO Zone LIHTC properties are eligible for enhanced credits of 91 percent instead of the normal 70 percent of qualified basis. Ninety-five percent of GO Zone private activity bond proceeds must be used for qualified projects. As of mid-June 2008, the three eligible states had allocated 87 percent of the $14.9 billion in private activity bond authority, and bonds issued equaled 44 percent of total authority; Alabama allocated 88 percent, Louisiana 89 percent, and Mississippi 84 percent. By state, the percentages allocated and issued were Alabama 39.5 percent, Louisiana 47.1 percent, and Mississippi 40.3 percent; percentages allocated only were Alabama 48.8 percent, Louisiana 41.8 percent, and Mississippi 44 percent; percentages unallocated were Alabama 11.7 percent, Louisiana 11.2 percent, and Mississippi 15.7 percent; the total percentages were 43.7 percent allocated and issued, 43.6 percent allocated only, and 12.7 percent unallocated. The 10 largest bonds issued accounted for approximately 92 percent of Alabama's, 76 percent of Louisiana's, and 69 percent of Mississippi's total bonds issued. Alabama awarded 7 percent of its authority to projects affecting multiple counties, Louisiana 6 percent, and Mississippi 29 percent. Mississippi's application fee was $1,000, and Louisiana later required a refundable deposit of 0.5 percent of the proposed allocation. As of April 2008, the five states had awarded 95 percent of the combined $330 million in LIHTCs; Florida, Mississippi, and Texas awarded all of the $113 million of additional GO Zone LIHTC allocations from 2006 through 2008, Alabama awarded 74 percent of its $47 million, and Louisiana awarded all of its allocation with some later returned. Planned and in-service GO Zone LIHTC-funded units as of April 2008 were: Alabama 3,259 planned and 68 in service; Florida 226 and 0; Louisiana 11,787 and 2,156; Mississippi 9,301 and 328; Texas 398 and 0. According to HUD data, over 82,000 rental housing units in Louisiana and over 20,000 in Mississippi had major or severe damage; nearly 80,000 were in eight Louisiana parishes and about 19,200 were in three Mississippi counties. Damaged units ranged from a low of 468 in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, to a high of nearly 52,000 in Orleans Parish, Louisiana. Planned and in-service GO Zone LIHTC-funded units are expected to address about 17 percent of rental housing units with major or severe damage in Louisiana and 45 percent in Mississippi. The percentages by selected parish or county were Calcasieu 64.0 percent, Cameron 5.4 percent, Vermillion 78.8 percent, Jefferson 7.2 percent, St. Tammany 20.2 percent, Orleans 16.7 percent, St. Bernard 0 percent, Plaquemines 0 percent, Hancock 25.6 percent, Harrison 30.5 percent, and Jackson 21.5 percent. Louisiana issued $200 million in tax credit bonds and Mississippi issued $100 million, exhausting the $350 million authority; Alabama did not issue any. The three states used 16 percent of the additional advance refunding authority. Alabama issued 65 advance refunding bonds and approved 19 more, totaling $599 million, about 53 percent of its authority; Louisiana issued 9 refundings totaling $483 million, about 11 percent; Mississippi issued 6 refundings totaling $169 million, about 8 percent. Louisiana's advance refunding bonds listed in the report were $154,425,000, $100,340,000, $70,000,000, $50,000,000, $44,258,396, $25,765,000, $20,000,000, $11,000,000, and $6,885,000. Mississippi's advance refunding bonds listed in the report were $125,000,000, $18,000,000, $15,000,000, $7,000,000, $2,000,000, and $1,500,000. All GO Zone private activity bonds and advance refunding bonds must be issued by December 31, 2010; tax credit bonds had to be issued by December 31, 2006 and retired within 2 years; and GO Zone LIHTC-funded units must be in service before January 1, 2011.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether all GO Zone LIHTC-funded units will be placed in service by the January 1, 2011 deadline; state officials anticipated that most would be, but identified challenges including the declining market value of tax credits, community resistance, environmental issues, and increased development costs. It also does not settle whether the most heavily damaged areas in and around New Orleans, Louisiana, will be able to use their designated GO Zone bond authority before it expires in 2010, or whether applicants with allocations will be able to issue bonds within required time frames. The report states that, due to differences in how bond type data were reported across the three eligible states, GAO did not attempt to quantify aggregate use by categories across the states. Comparable data on rental housing units with major or severe damage were not available for every GO Zone parish and county in Louisiana and Mississippi, or for Alabama, Florida, or Texas. GAO did not assess the extent to which LIHTC compliance monitoring policies have been followed because few GO Zone LIHTC-funded units had been placed in service as of April 2008. The report also notes that other programs can fund affordable rental housing, so the 17 percent and 45 percent figures address only GO Zone LIHTC-funded units. State officials expressed uncertainty about whether GO Zone bonds should be used quickly anywhere within the qualified areas or focused more narrowly on the most damaged areas, and Louisiana's Department of Economic Development review acknowledged that Louisiana's GO Zone bond process lacked effective prioritization and viability mechanisms and that changing rules had caused disappointment and confusion.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Finance and the Chairman and Ranking Member of the House Committee on Ways and Means; it is a mandated report to Congress to support congressional oversight and decisions about GO Zone tax incentive allocation and use.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a July 31, 2008, U.S. Government Accountability Office follow-up audit report, GAO-08-918, on the Department of Veterans Affairs' progress in strengthening controls over information technology equipment. It responds to a request from the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, to determine whether VA has made progress in implementing prior GAO recommendations and whether VA's current internal controls are effective in preventing theft, loss, or misappropriation of IT equipment. The scope includes VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory of IT equipment, statistical tests of IT inventory controls at three VA health care systems (North Texas, Puget Sound, and Boston) and VA headquarters, controls over hard drives in the disposal process, and physical security of IT storage locations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that VA made significant progress in addressing prior recommendations: as of July 2008, VA had completed action on 10 of 12 recommendations from GAO's July 2007 report, partially implemented one, and had actions under way on the remaining one; VA completed action on 4 of 6 property-related recommendations from the July 2004 report, partially completed one, and had plans to address the remaining one. VA's new Handbook 7002, mandated for early implementation on July 3, 2008, includes requirements for user-level accountability, time frames for Reports of Survey, and strengthened physical security. VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory initially found approximately 79,000 missing IT equipment items; as of May 15, 2008, approximately 62,800 recorded items could not be located, of which over 9,800 could have stored sensitive information. GAO's statistical tests at four case study locations from February through May 2008 identified 50 missing items, including 34 that could have stored sensitive personal and medical information, despite excluding thousands of items already identified as missing in VA's inventory. Estimated inventory control failure rates for missing items were 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS, 3 percent at Boston HCS, 6 percent at North Texas HCS, and 12 percent for VA headquarters organizations. GAO also found continuing weaknesses in user-level accountability, inventory record accuracy, controls over hard drives in the disposal process, and physical security of IT storage facilities, and found that medical equipment with data storage capabilities was not included in VA's 2007 IT physical inventory.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Key figures from the report include: GAO-08-918, issued July 31, 2008, 52 pages. As of September 30, 2007, VA reported over 230,000 employees. VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory initially identified approximately 79,000 missing IT equipment items; as of May 15, 2008, OIT reported approximately 62,800 recorded IT equipment items could not be located, and table 3 shows a total of 62,880 missing items and 9,866 open Report of Survey items that could have stored sensitive data. Over 9,800 missing items could have stored sensitive information. As of May 15, 2008, VA had over 43,000 items on open Reports of Survey. GAO's statistical tests at four case study locations identified 50 missing items, of which 34 could have stored sensitive information. Estimated missing-item control failure rates were 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS, 3 percent at Boston HCS, 6 percent at North Texas HCS, and 12 percent for VA headquarters organizations. Other estimated failure rates at the four locations were: blank serial numbers, 59 percent at North Texas HCS, 17 percent at Boston HCS, 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS, and 1 percent at VA headquarters; incorrect user organization, 91 percent, 60 percent, 76 percent, and 12 percent respectively; incorrect user location, 46 percent, 17 percent, 14 percent, and 33 percent; and total recordkeeping failures, 9 percent, 41 percent, 9 percent, and 4 percent. Population sizes tested were 12,172 IT equipment items at North Texas HCS, 15,706 at Boston HCS, 11,474 at Puget Sound HCS, and 34,735 at VA headquarters organizations. In table 4, missing items identified during the 2007 VA-wide inventory that were not located as of May 15, 2008 were 5,308 at North Texas HCS, 1,269 at Puget Sound HCS, 3,226 at Boston HCS, and 1,314 at VA headquarters; missing items as of May 15, 2008 that could have stored sensitive information were 3,351, 443, 725, and 608 respectively. VA completed action on 10 of 12 recommendations from the July 2007 report and 4 of 6 property-related recommendations from the July 2004 report. At VA headquarters, GAO found 147 errors out of 349 records tested, and received 20 hand receipts for 38 mobile IT equipment items requested, with 4 dated after the request date and 16 valid; no receipts were received for 18 devices. At North Texas HCS, 7,164 of 12,172 recorded IT equipment items, about 59 percent, did not have serial numbers recorded. An excess property storage room at North Texas HCS contained boxes of 86 hard drives needing disposal or sanitization. At Puget Sound HCS, approximately 100 hard drives observed had been in storage for approximately 3 or 4 years. At Boston HCS, some hard drives dated back to the 1980's.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommended that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs require the CIO, with the support of medical centers and VA headquarters organizations tested and other VA organizations, as appropriate, to take five actions: review property inventory records and confirm that all IT equipment, regardless of the organizational equipment inventory listing, is identified in the property system; establish and implement a policy requiring development of standardized naming classifications for IT equipment, including item name, manufacturer, and model, for recording IT equipment into local property inventory systems; develop a list of medical equipment with data storage capability that should be considered as IT equipment for inventory control purposes; develop a procedure for identifying hard drive serial numbers with both the property identification numbers and serial numbers of host computers; and revise the definition of IT storage locations in VA's Handbook 0730/1, Security and Law Enforcement, to include informal IT storage locations, such as OIT work rooms, and require these locations to be included in physical security inspections. The report notes that VA initially generally agreed with four of the five recommendations and, after clarification, agreed with the intent of all five.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: GAO stated that it did not validate the results of VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory.
