about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines rebaselining of the federal government's major information technology (IT) projects: it determines the extent of and primary reasons for IT project rebaselining and whether agencies have sound policies for rebaselining projects. The scope covers the 24 major federal agencies and the 778 major IT projects they planned to invest in during fiscal year 2008, based on a survey of a random sample of 180 projects and a comparison of agency policies to best practices in GAO's Cost Assessment Guide.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that an estimated 48 percent of the federal government's major IT projects have been rebaselined, that projects are rebaselined for several reasons including changes in project goals and changes in funding, and that rebaselining can result in significant changes to cost and schedule goals. It also finds that although all 24 major agencies have established rebaselining policies, none of the policies are fully consistent with the five best practices identified in GAO's Cost Assessment Guide, and that agencies' policies vary in part because the Office of Management and Budget has not issued guidance specifying what elements these policies should include.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The federal government planned to spend about $70 billion on information technology projects during fiscal year 2008, on 778 major projects at 24 major agencies. GAO surveyed a random sample of 180 projects and achieved a response rate of 99 percent. The report's text estimates that about 48 percent of major IT projects have been rebaselined; figure 1 displays Rebaselined: 49%; Not rebaselined: 51%. Of rebaselined projects, about 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice and about 11 percent were rebaselined 4 times or more. The most commonly cited reason for the most recent rebaselining was change in project requirements, objectives, or scope, at 55 percent; change in funding stream was cited at 44 percent; original baseline was inaccurate at 14 percent; cost or schedule overruns due to project performance at 4 percent; cost or schedule overruns due to contractor performance at 4 percent; and other at 41 percent. Figure 2 shows the estimated frequency of times rebaselined as: 1 time, 49 percent; 2 times, 29 percent; 3 times, 11 percent; 4 times, 5 percent; 5 times, 4 percent; 6 times, 1 percent; 7 times, 1 percent. Table 1 lists nine projects rebaselined four or more times: Advanced Field Artillery Tactical Data System, 4; Licensing Support Network, 4; Coast Guard Rescue 21, 4; Integrated Human Resources and Training System, 4; Program Fund Control System, 5; Patent and Trade Office Revenue and Account Management System, 5; Commerce Business Environment, 5; Health Admin Center IT Operations, 6; and Tenant Rental Assistance Certification System, 7. Table 3 reports in millions of dollars: National Polar-orbiting Operational Environmental Satellite System original cost $7000, cost after rebaseline(s) $12500, dollar change $5500, percent change 79%, original completion date 2018, completion date after rebaseline 2026, delay 8 years; Navy Enterprise Resource Planning original cost $1993, cost after rebaseline(s) $2445, dollar change $452, percent change 23%, original completion date Jun. 2011, completion date after rebaseline Aug. 2013, delay 2.2 years; FAA Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System original cost $940, cost after rebaseline(s) $2770, dollar change $1830, percent change 195%, original completion date Oct. 2005, completion date after rebaseline Dec. 2007, delay 2.2 years; FAA Wide Area Augmentation System original cost $1001, cost after rebaseline(s) $3340, dollar change $2339, percent change 234%, original completion date Aug. 1999, completion date after rebaseline Dec. 2008, delay 9.3 years; US Coast Guard Rescue 21 original cost $250, cost after rebaseline(s) $711, dollar change $461, percent change 184%, original completion date 2006, completion date after rebaseline 2011, delay 5 years. Policy assessments show that none of the agencies' policies fully addressed all five practices; 79 percent fully or partially addressed describing reasons when a rebaseline is warranted, 96 percent fully or partially addressed requiring management review, 88 percent fully or partially addressed requiring that the process is documented, while 46 percent of policies did not address describing the process for developing a new baseline and 54 percent did not address requiring validation of the new baseline. Table 4 reports full, partial, and not addressed counts: describe reasons when a rebaseline is warranted, 14 (58%), 5 (21%), 5 (21%); describe process for developing a new baseline, 0 (0%), 13 (54%), 11 (46%); require validating the new baseline, 5 (21%), 6 (25%), 13 (54%); require management review, 9 (38%), 14 (58%), 1 (4%); require that the process is documented, 6 (25%), 15 (63%), 3 (13%).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of OMB issue guidance for rebaselining policies that would include a minimum set of key elements, taking into consideration the criteria used in this report, and that each of the heads of the 24 major agencies direct the development of comprehensive rebaselining policies that address the weaknesses GAO identified.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that all proportion estimates from the sample used in this report have 95 percent confidence intervals of within plus or minus 11 percentage points, unless otherwise noted. It also notes that OMB has not issued guidance specifying what elements agencies' rebaselining policies are to include, and that OMB officials acknowledged they had not established specific criteria to evaluate agencies' earned value management policies and that having such criteria would improve consistency. The report notes that rebaselining can be used to mask cost overruns and schedule delays, but it does not present findings that any specific rebaselining was so used. It also includes the caveat that only a portion of the National Polar-orbiting Operational Environmental Satellite System's costs are included in the federal government's $70 billion estimated IT expenditures for fiscal year 2008 and the rest is not considered to be an IT investment.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional requesters, issued July 28, 2008, with the report number GAO-08-954. It examines progress made by the Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs in developing electronic health record systems or capabilities that allow full interoperability of personal health care information between the departments, steps taken to ensure compliance with applicable federal interoperability standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria, and efforts to establish the joint interagency program office required by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008. It is the first in a series of semi-annual GAO reports required by that act.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DOD and VA have established and implemented mechanisms to achieve interoperable sharing of some, but not all, electronic health information, and that information is shared at different levels of interoperability. Pharmacy and drug allergy data on shared patients are exchanged in computable form, the highest level; viewable data shared include microbiology results, cytology reports, chemistry and hematology reports, and other items. Not all electronic health information is yet shared; examples are immunization records and history, data on exposure to health hazards, and psychological health treatment and care records. Also, although VA's health information is all captured electronically, not all health data collected by DOD are electronic; many DOD medical facilities use paper-based health records. The departments have agreed on common standards and participate in federal standards initiatives, and they have taken steps to establish the joint interagency program office, but the office does not yet have permanent leadership, staff, or facilities, and the draft implementation plan still has milestone dates to be determined despite the September 2009 deadline. GAO recommended that the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs give priority to fully establishing the office and finalizing the draft implementation plan; both departments concurred.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is 48 pages and was issued July 28, 2008. As of June 2008, outpatient pharmacy and drug allergy data were being exchanged on more than 18,300 shared patients. Under the BHIE interface, clinicians can view data from 17 DOD sites (about 40 percent of inpatient beds) and all VA sites. The Laboratory Data Sharing Interface is deployed at nine locations. Under the Consolidated Health Informatics initiative, DOD, VA, and other agencies agreed to endorse 20 sets of standards. In developing interoperability specifications for the three initial use cases, HITSP examined and assessed more than 700 existing standards and identified 30 named standards. In 2006, the Certification Commission certified the first 37 ambulatory electronic health record products; to date it has certified over 100 electronic health record products. The American Health Information Community is an 18-member body with high-level representatives from DOD and VA. The Target DOD/VA Health Standards Profile is dated September 2007. DOD's AHLTA version 3.3 was conditionally certified in April 2007 against 2006 outpatient electronic health record criteria and has been beta tested at three DOD locations. The departments requested $4.94 million to fund the joint interagency program office for fiscal year 2008 and submitted funding requirements of $6.94 million for fiscal year 2009 in June. About 30 permanent staff are expected for the office. Of 52 milestone dates for Interoperability II in the draft implementation plan, 19 are yet to be determined. The draft implementation plan was dated April 25, 2008, almost 2 months after the February 28, 2008 due date. The program office is expected to be fully operational by December 2008, leaving 9 months before the September 2009 goal.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs give priority to fully establishing the Joint Interagency Program Office by expediting efforts to put in place permanent leadership, staff, and facilities, and to make the necessary decisions to finalize the draft implementation plan. The departments concurred with these recommendations; DOD stated it would give high priority to fully establishing the office, and VA described planned actions including appointing a permanent Deputy Director by October 2008 and hiring permanent program staff by December 2008.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that DOD and VA cannot yet share all essential health information, and it names immunization records and history, data on exposure to health hazards, and psychological health treatment and care records as examples not yet shared. It also states that the departments are unable to track the number of shared patients currently receiving care from both departments, so the number of patients for whom data could potentially be shared is unknown. DOD medical facilities' paper-based records and TRICARE clinical encounters not captured in DOD's electronic health system unless care is received at a military treatment facility are noted as remaining limitations. The DOD/VA Information Interoperability Plan is still in draft, has not been assessed by GAO, and, if it includes the essential elements needed, could improve prospects for success; the requirements for Interoperability II enhancements have not been fully defined, and 19 of 52 milestone dates are yet to be determined, with decisions depending on clinical priorities, technical considerations, and policy decisions. The departments have not made a decision on a joint inpatient system; recommendations on possible approaches were expected at the end of July 2008. GAO has not yet fully assessed the Office of the National Coordinator's June 2008 four-year strategic plan. The scope of the joint interagency program office may broaden to include sharing personnel and benefits data, and AHLTA version 3.3 cannot be fully certified until the commission verifies it has been in operational use at a medical site.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees listed in the letter—the subcommittees and committees on Defense Appropriations, Military Construction and Veterans' Affairs Appropriations, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs—to support congressional oversight of DOD and VA progress toward fully interoperable electronic health records as required by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO-08-955, July 2008) describes a covert undercover operation in which GAO investigators created two fictitious durable medical equipment suppliers, one in Maryland and one in Virginia, to test Medicare's DMEPOS supplier enrollment and screening process. It covers GAO's success in obtaining Medicare billing numbers and completing electronic test billing, the weaknesses found in CMS's and the National Supplier Clearinghouse's verification of the 25 supplier standards, and four closed South Florida fraud cases provided by the HHS Inspector General.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that CMS approved both fictitious DMEPOS storefronts even though they had no clients and no inventory. Although CMS and NSC initially denied the applications because the companies did not demonstrate compliance with Standards 4 and 14, both were approved after GAO resubmitted phony wholesale supplier contracts and repair policies. NSC performed limited verification of those contracts; when NSC called the phony wholesaler's telephone number, an undercover investigator left a vague return message and NSC did no further follow-up. GAO successfully completed Medicare's test billing for the Virginia office with a test file of 27 claims and no errors, but did not complete test billing for Maryland because the necessary passwords were not received by the close of the investigation. GAO also found, from HHS IG case studies, that criminals use similar techniques to bill Medicare for millions, and concluded that, had the operation continued, it could have fraudulently billed substantial sums, potentially reaching millions of dollars. CMS acknowledged that the covert testing showed gaps in oversight that still require improvement and said it is implementing new supplier requirements.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that Medicare helps pay for services on behalf of almost 42 million elderly and certain disabled beneficiaries. In December 2006, HHS IG randomly visited 1,581 DMEPOS suppliers in South Florida and found almost one-third had no office at the address they provided Medicare, though they had collectively submitted claims for hundreds of millions of dollars. CMS estimated that, from April 2006 through March 2007, $1 billion of the $10 billion Medicare paid for DMEPOS supplies were improper. GAO's two office rentals cost approximately $1,000 per month; state business licenses cost about $400 per supplier; GAO purchased approximately $3 million of general liability insurance at a cost of $550 annually. GAO's Maryland application took about 9 months and was approved effective February 13, 2008; the Virginia application took about 6 months and was approved retroactive to September 28, 2007. On May 14, 2008, GAO successfully submitted a test file with 27 claims for $6,876.34 with no errors. In the case studies, one owner submitted about $1.5 million in claims from January 1, 2006 through April 30, 2007, Medicare paid $372,286, and she was sentenced to 30 months imprisonment and 3 years supervised release and ordered to pay $372,286 in restitution. Another owner submitted claims in excess of $5.5 million from October 2006 through March 2007 and received about $77,000; he was sentenced to 37 months in prison, ordered to pay over $70,000 in restitution, and had to forfeit his Miami home and Rolls Royce. A company billed Medicare for $4.4 million in supplies and services that were never delivered, with claims submitted between March and July 2006, and Medicare paid about $2.2 million; the owner was sentenced to 4 years in prison and 3 years of probation, assessed a $100 fee, and ordered to pay $2.2 million in restitution. Another owner bought Medicare beneficiary numbers illegally for $45 each, billed over $1 million from July 2005 through October 2006, received over $500,000 in payments, and was ordered to pay $702,186 in restitution and sentenced to 2 years in federal prison and 3 years of probation.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether the new accreditation process, revised and additional supplier standards, and competitive bidding will close the gaps it identified; it states these actions will only be successful if those tasked with ensuring compliance exercise due diligence when conducting screenings and inspections. It also notes that GAO did not complete test billing for the Maryland company because it did not receive the necessary passwords from CMS by the close of the investigation in June 2008, and that GAO used fictitious beneficiaries and physician identification numbers found on the Internet only to complete test billing, without compromising the provider status of legitimate physicians or the status of actual beneficiaries. In one case, CMS confirmed that a fictitious physician number should not have passed the initial computer system edit for payment.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-981R, issued August 15, 2008) examines DOD's programs to promote positive working relationships between reservists and their employers. It covers whether DOD has informed reservists of their obligation to provide employers advance notice of active-duty calls, DOD initiatives to improve reservist-employer relations, and whether there has been a reduction in the hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001 because of increased reserve use or DOD policy changes. It was prepared for four congressional committees at the direction of the Military Reservists and Veteran Small Business Reauthorization and Opportunity Act of 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: DOD has taken steps to inform reservists of their obligations and responsibilities to their civilian employers, including policies encouraging written advance notice and ESGR outreach, but it does not collect data to assess the effectiveness of these efforts. DOD has used ESGR as its focal point for a strategic approach to promote positive working relationships, but ESGR lacks an established performance plan, a follow-up mechanism for employers who have signed statements of support, and an outreach program specific to small businesses, even though small business employers represent nearly 70 percent of selected reservists' employers. GAO was unable to determine whether there has been a reduction in the hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001 because of a lack of available data and analyses, and the focus group and employer interview results were based on nonprobability samples and are not generalizable.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Since September 11, 2001, DOD has relied on more than 650,000 members of the National Guard and Reserve. For fiscal year 2008, ESGR has a budget of approximately $13.1 million. In fiscal year 2007, more than 67,000 employers and approximately 235,000 reservists were briefed on USERRA and ESGR services; ESGR field committees briefed 68,803 employers; 15,124 employers were nominated for the Patriot Award; more than 1,000 reservists nominated their employers for the Freedom Award; and more than 20,644 employers signed statements of support. According to a 2006 DOD Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 79 percent of reservists responding said they had been briefed on USERRA at least once. According to the 2007 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 76 percent of reservists had received an informal alert notice; of those, an estimated 77 percent received notice of 30 days or more, and an estimated 47 percent received written, formal orders 30 days or more prior to having to report for active duty. A November 2007 DOD report to Congress found that nearly 70 percent of employers of selected reservists have fewer than 100 employees. ESGR has 36 military employees, 28 civilian employees, 8 contractors, and 94 contractor field support personnel, and operates through more than 4,500 volunteers throughout 56 committees. GAO conducted 10 focus groups in three states with 50 volunteer participants, selected 77 employers, and completed interviews with 11 employers. DOD's comments report that ESGR Ombudsman Service contacts increased from 5,298 in FY05 to 7,765 in FY06 to 13,116 in FY07 to 8,575 in FY08 as of June 30, while actual cases decreased from 4,682 in FY05 to 3,152 in FY06 to 2,374 in FY07 to 1,988 in FY08, and employers signing statements of support increased from 10,909 in FY05 to 11,396 in FY06 to 20,644 in FY07 to 27,770 in FY08 as of June 30. ESGR's strategic plan set a goal to obtain statements of support from 100 percent of identified civilian employers by 2011, which equates to obtaining an average of 20 percent of these employers in each year of the period covered by the plan.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness to establish an annual performance plan that develops and facilitates the implementation of performance measures on how well ESGR is achieving its goals, to conduct regular and recurring follow-up activities on outreach efforts to maintain positive working relationships with employers who have previously signed statements of support, and to develop initiatives to specifically conduct outreach efforts to small businesses that employ reservists. The report notes that DOD partially concurred with these three recommendations. A fourth draft recommendation, to add questions to DOD's Status of Forces Surveys about the amount and form of notice reservists provide to employers, was omitted from the final report because Defense Manpower Data Center officials said they were planning to include such questions.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether there has been a reduction in the hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001. It states that GAO was unable to determine this due to a lack of available data, that no studies or analyses from DOD or the Department of Labor were identified, and that even if a reduction had occurred, GAO would be unable to determine what factors contributed to it. The document also states that DOD does not collect data on the amount or form of advance notice reservists provide to their employers, so it cannot determine the effectiveness of its USERRA education efforts. It notes that the focus groups and employer interviews were based on nonprobability samples and are not generalizable, and that it is difficult to establish a direct causal link between ESGR's outreach efforts and their effectiveness.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-992, issued September 9, 2008) examines TSA's requirements for domestic air carriers to conduct watch-list matching against the No Fly and Selectee lists for domestic flights, and the extent to which TSA has assessed air carriers' compliance with those requirements. It covers TSA's security directives, air carriers' similar-name-matching practices, TSA inspections and special emphasis assessments, and TSA's expectation that Secure Flight, scheduled to begin implementation in January 2009, is the ultimate solution.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key findings are that, before the April 2008 revision, TSA's security directives required similar-name matching but did not specify how many or what types of name variations air carriers had to compare; the 14 air carriers GAO interviewed used varied approaches, so a passenger could be identified as a match by one carrier and not another. TSA had conducted limited testing of similar-name matching until a January 2008 special emphasis inspection; the 2005 special emphasis assessment tested exact-name matching only, and in fiscal year 2007 documented name-matching tests appeared in 6 of 36 principal security inspector inspections and 55 of 1,109 transportation security inspector inspections. The January 2008 inspection of 83 air carriers using 100 No Fly List names found that no air carrier identified matches involving all types of name variations. In response, TSA revised the No Fly List security directive in April 2008 to establish a baseline similar-name-matching capability and planned to revise the Selectee List directive similarly, while stating that Secure Flight, expected to begin implementation in January 2009, is the ultimate solution.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is 58 pages and was issued September 9, 2008. As of that date, it was more than 6 years after the September 11, 2001 attacks. TSA documented several known incidents involving No Fly List individuals on international flights for the 3-year period from January 2005 through December 2007. GAO interviewed officials from 14 domestic air carriers; 8 were major air carriers and the remaining 6 had smaller operations, and the 14 carriers accounted for approximately 70 percent of all passengers who boarded domestic flights in 2005. As of January 2008, 9 principal security inspectors were responsible for domestic air carriers; for fiscal year 2007, 72 domestic air carriers were subject to the No Fly and Selectee list security directives. As of June 2008, 681 transportation security inspectors covered 459 commercial airports. In fiscal year 2007, TSA conducted 1,145 watch-list-related inspections: 1,109 at airports by transportation security inspectors and 36 at corporate security offices by principal security inspectors; they covered 60 of the 72 carriers, and TSA found compliance in 1,133 (99 percent) of the 1,145 inspections. Name-matching tests were documented in 55 of the 1,109 airport inspections and in 6 of the 36 corporate inspections; 6 of TSA's 9 principal security inspectors said their assessments had not included examining certain basic similar-name comparisons. TSA's January 2008 special emphasis inspection was a 3-day inspection of 83 air carriers—52 domestic and 31 foreign—using 100 names on the No Fly List. TSA's 2005 special emphasis assessment was conducted in June, July, and September 2005. After the April 2008 revision, TSA estimated air carriers would need 2 to 4 weeks to implement the new requirements, and TSA said contracting with third-party vendors could take almost 2 years. Of the 14 air carriers interviewed, 10 said more similar-name comparisons produce more potential matches and 12 said large numbers of potential matches can cause congestion at ticket counters. A May 20–29, 2008 special emphasis assessment checked 7 air carriers' compliance with the revised No Fly List security directive. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2008 requires GAO to report on DHS certification of 10 conditions, with the report due 90 days after the Secretary certifies them. Air carriers must compare passenger data within 24 hours of scheduled flight departure and keep selectee records for 7 calendar days. TSA expects Secure Flight to begin implementation in January 2009.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that the results of GAO's telephone interviews with 14 air carriers are not generalizable to all domestic air carriers, and GAO did not independently verify each carrier's reported method of implementation. TSA's 2005 special emphasis assessment used sampling and related procedures that were insufficient for a reliable estimate of the success rate of all attempted matches, and its findings cannot be used to infer overall or individual compliance rates. GAO did not assess the reliability of data from the January 2008 special emphasis inspection or the May 2008 special emphasis assessment. Data on false negative watch-list-matching results generally are not available for domestic flights, so the extent of domestic carriers' failures is difficult to determine. TSA officials acknowledged that the new baseline capability does not address all vulnerabilities identified by TSA; TSA could not provide data or analysis supporting its assertion that requiring comparisons beyond the baseline was not warranted, and GAO did not independently analyze the sufficiency of the baseline or the option of expanding the lists. The details of the May 2008 special emphasis assessment are classified, and it is too early to determine the extent to which TSA will assess carriers' compliance with the revised requirements. GAO also reported that Secure Flight's life-cycle cost and schedule estimates did not fully follow best practices, putting the program at risk of cost overruns, missed deadlines, and performance shortfalls.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is addressed to the congressional committees listed in it—Senate and House committees on Appropriations, Commerce, Science, and Transportation, Homeland Security, the Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Oversight and Government Reform—to support their oversight of TSA's watch-list matching and Secure Flight implementation.
